howItWorks.title: How text to speech works here
howItWorks.p1: Type or paste text, pick a voice, and press Generate: the text is spoken by the same neural voices Microsoft Edge uses for Read Aloud and comes back as an MP3 you can play or save. There are 322 voices across 75 languages and 142 regional variants, Bangla among them.
howItWorks.example: Hello there. [pause 2s] This is after two seconds. [pause 0.5s] And a short one. → an 8.7-second, 51 KB MP3 in the Jenny voice, with the silences where the markers were
howItWorks.p2: The one thing to know before you start: the text leaves your browser. It goes through this site's server to Microsoft's service, which does the speaking, and this site keeps no copy of it or of the audio. Documents opened on the File to Speech tab are read in your browser, and only the text you then generate from is sent.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is it free?
faq.a1: Yes. There is no account and no charge. The hourly limits are there so one heavy user cannot spend everybody's share.
faq.q2: Can I use the audio commercially?
faq.a2: This site makes no claim on the audio, but the voices are Microsoft's, and whether a recording may be used commercially is a question for Microsoft's terms rather than this page. For anything you will publish or sell, check those terms, or use a licensed speech service.
faq.q3: Why does the text from my PDF come out as nonsense?
faq.a3: A PDF records which shapes to draw where, not always which letters they are. For Latin text the two usually line up; for Bangla, Hindi, Arabic and other scripts that join or reorder characters, the extracted text is often scrambled. Copy the text from the original document instead, or save it as .docx or .odt and open that.
faq.q4: Why is there a pause I did not add?
faq.a4: Long text is sent in parts of about 4 KB, cut at a line break or a full stop where possible, and each part ends with the voice's own short silence. At the end of a sentence it is the same breath the voice would take anyway.
faq.q5: Can it read Bangla?
faq.a5: Yes, with four voices: Nabanita and Pradeep for Bangladesh, Tanishaa and Bashkar for India. With the site in Bangla, the page opens on Nabanita.
faq.q6: Why do I have to pass a bot check?
faq.a6: Because every generation is a request to a shared service from this site's address. The check stops scripts from using the page as a free speech API, which would get that address throttled for everyone.
faq.q7: How long can the text be?
faq.a7: Up to 10,000 characters per generation, markers included, and 30 generations an hour from one address. For a long document, generate it a chapter at a time.
faq.a8: No. The service accepts only the plain text Edge itself sends — markup such as '<'break> is refused outright, which is why pauses are markers in the text instead.
faq.q9: Can it translate my text before reading it?
faq.a9: Yes. Pick a voice in the language you want, then press Translate: the box is translated into that language by Google Translate, with pause markers untouched, and Undo translation brings your original back. It only happens when you press the button.

whatItIs.title: What this does
whatItIs.p1: This page finds the text in a picture — a screenshot, a photographed page, a sign, a scanned form — and gives it back as text you can edit and copy. It reads printed text in eight languages, from English and Spanish to Bangla, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese and Japanese.
whatItIs.example: 这 是 中 文, as the engine reads it → 这是中文, as the box hands it to you
whatItIs.p2: Choose the language before you add the picture: it decides which alphabet the engine looks for, and English is read alongside every choice. Nothing is uploaded — the picture is read in this tab, and the only download is the engine itself, once.

uploaded.question: Is my picture uploaded?
uploaded.answer: No. It is read in this tab by Tesseract compiled to WebAssembly. The only network traffic is the engine and language data from jsDelivr on first use — unless you import the picture by link, which this server fetches for you.

firstRun.question: Why is the first read slower?
firstRun.answer: It downloads the engine and the language data first, 7 to 9 MB in all. The browser keeps them, so the next read in the same language starts straight away.

handwriting.question: Can it read handwriting?
handwriting.answer: Not reliably. The models are trained on printed text. Neat capitals sometimes work; joined-up writing does not.

nonsense.question: Why is my text full of nonsense characters?
nonsense.answer: Usually the language is wrong — the engine reads the alphabet it was given. Pick the language the text is in and press Read again. If the language is right, try a sharper, straighter crop.

mixed.question: Can it read a picture with two languages?
mixed.answer: English is read alongside every language, so Bangla with English words in it, or Arabic with English brand names, works in one read. For two languages other than English, read the picture twice, once in each.

several.question: Can I read several pictures at once?
several.answer: Yes — up to {count, number} in one go, read one after another by a single copy of the engine. By default each picture's text gets its own box beside the picture; switch Text layout to Combined to get all of it in one box, each picture's text under a heading with its number and file name, in the order you added them.

pdf.question: Does it read a PDF?
pdf.answer: Not directly — it reads pictures. Take a screenshot of the page and drop that in.

understanding.title: What makes a password strong
understanding.p1: A password is strong when it is hard to guess, and nothing else. Not when it has a capital letter, not when it has a symbol, not when it satisfies a form's validation rules — those were written to nudge people away from dragon and 123456, and what they mostly produced was Dragon1!.
understanding.example: 6 words → candle-anchor-copper-piano-amber-tide — exactly 60 bits, because the list holds exactly 1024 words and every word is one uniform draw from it
understanding.p2: What actually resists guessing is unpredictability, and a person cannot supply it: human-chosen passwords cluster in the same few shapes, and an attacker's dictionary knows every one of them. So the useful question is never how a password looks but how many equally likely results the thing that made it could have produced instead — which is the number reported beside every result here. Every character and every word is drawn in your browser by crypto.getRandomValues, and nothing on this page is ever transmitted.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is it safe to generate a password on a website?
faq.a1: On this one the password is never transmitted: it is composed in your browser by the platform's cryptographic generator and stays there. You do still have to trust that the page you loaded is the page we published, which is the trust any web tool asks for. If you would rather not extend it, a local password manager's generator does the same job — the arithmetic on this page is here so you can check that whatever you use is telling you the truth.
faq.q2: Where does the randomness come from?
faq.a2: crypto.getRandomValues, the browser's cryptographically secure generator, seeded by the operating system. Math.random is never used anywhere in this tool: it is fast and predictable, and a predictable password generator is not one. Selections use rejection sampling rather than a modulo, so no character in the pool is very slightly more likely than another.
faq.q3: How accurate is the crack-time figure?
faq.a3: The keyspace is exact — counted rather than estimated, including the cost of guaranteeing one character per class. The guess rate is rounded to a power of ten, because it depends on the attacker's hardware and on the hash the target chose, and both change. So read the result as an order of magnitude against the scenario you picked. The distance between the four scenarios tells you far more than the digits inside any one of them.
faq.q4: Why is a six-digit PIN called very weak?
faq.a4: Because there are only a million of them, and a machine allowed to try them offline finishes before you let go of the mouse. That is not a flaw in the PIN, it is what a PIN is. It works because the phone or card behind it locks after a few wrong tries, not because the number is hard to guess — so never use one where an attacker can guess as fast as they like.
faq.q5: Is a passphrase really as strong as random characters?
faq.a5: It can be, but it takes more of it. Six words from the 1024-word list is sixty bits; ten random characters across all four classes is about sixty-six. The trade is memorability against length, and a passphrase you can hold in your head beats a stronger one you write on a sticky note. For anything a manager remembers for you, use random characters.
faq.q6: Why does capitalising the words not make it stronger?
faq.a6: Because it is a rule, and an attacker searching this keyspace applies the same rule for free. Upper-casing the first letter of every word turns one candidate into exactly one different candidate — the set does not grow. Any transformation you could describe in a sentence costs them nothing. Only choices made at random count, which is why the digit option adds bits and the capitalisation option does not.
faq.q7: Can I reuse a strong password across sites?
faq.a7: No. Strength protects against guessing, and reuse is not a guessing problem: when a site is breached and had stored passwords badly, the attacker gets yours directly and tries it on your email. A unique password per account is the highest-value habit here, and it is only practical with a manager.

understanding.title: A key is not a password
understanding.p1: Both are secrets, and that is where the resemblance ends. A password is remembered and typed by a person, which is why it is short, why it is guessable, and why it has to be stored behind a deliberately slow hash like bcrypt or argon2. A key is never remembered and never typed — it is written once into a config file and read back by a machine. Nothing about it needs to be memorable, so nothing about it needs to be weak.
understanding.p2: That changes what you generate. There is no reason to draw a key from a keyboard alphabet, and no reason to stop at a length somebody would be willing to type. You draw bytes, as many as the algorithm wants, and then you decide how to write them down.
understanding.example: {command} → {characters, number} characters carrying exactly {bits, number} bits
understanding.p3: That line is the reason most people arrive here. It draws 32 bytes, prints them as base64, swaps the two characters a URL would object to, and strips the padding. The tool above is the same three steps with the pieces named and each one turned into a control.
understanding.p4: Where does a key like that go? AUTH_SECRET, a JWT signing secret, a session cookie key, a CSRF token, a webhook signing secret, an API key you issue, or the key for a symmetric cipher. Every one of them wants the same thing: a value nobody can predict, in a form the surrounding file will accept unchanged.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is openssl rand -base64 32 still fine?
faq.a1: Yes — it is a good command, and it is what this tool is modelled on. Two things about it are worth knowing: without {swap} the output can contain + and /, which a URL percent-encodes, and above 48 bytes openssl wraps its output at 64 characters, putting a newline inside the key.
faq.q2: Why 32 bytes?
faq.a2: Because it is the key size HMAC-SHA256, AES-256 and ChaCha20 all specify, so one number answers nearly every question that brings somebody here. Below 16 bytes the key becomes the weakest part of the system; above 32, nothing on that list can use the extra.
faq.q3: What is the difference between base64 and base64url?
faq.a3: Two characters. Standard base64's 62nd and 63rd symbols are + and /; base64url uses - and _ instead. Everything else is identical, the entropy included — which is why switching between them here respells the key rather than drawing a new one.
faq.q4: Can I use this for a password?
faq.a4: You can, and it will be a very strong one, but it will also be unmemorable and painful to type. The Password Generator is the tool for a value a person has to enter by hand; this one is for a value only a machine ever reads.
faq.q5: Is the key ever sent to the server?
faq.a5: No. It is drawn in your browser tab by the Web Crypto API and never leaves it. The page arrives with a placeholder rather than a key, precisely so that no secret ever sits inside an HTTP response body.
faq.q6: Why does changing the encoding not give me a new key?
faq.a6: Because the encoding is a question about how to write the value down, not a request for a different value. Redrawing there would make it impossible to see one key as base64url and then as hex, which is most of what the encoding control is for. The New key button and the byte count are what draw again.
faq.q7: What does the padding switch actually change?
faq.a7: The trailing = characters, and nothing else. They carry no information — they exist so a strict decoder knows where a block ended. Keep them if the consumer insists on them; drop them if the key is going into a URL, where each one becomes %3D.

understanding.title: What a QR code actually holds
understanding.p1: A QR code is a grid of black and white squares, called modules, that encodes bytes. Nothing more. The three large squares in the corners tell a scanner where the code is and which way up it sits; the rest is data, error-correction codewords, and a handful of fields describing how to read them.
understanding.example: WIFI:T:WPA;S:Cafe;P:hunter2;; → a phone offers to join the network, because the prefix is a convention scanners agree on
understanding.p2: Because the payload is only bytes, the meaning of a code is a convention between whoever wrote it and whoever reads it — WIFI: offers a network, BEGIN:VCARD offers a contact — which is why picking the right type matters more than it looks. The grid itself comes in {versions, number} sizes, called versions, from 21 modules across up to 177; this tool picks the smallest one your content fits into, so a short link stays a coarse, forgiving code rather than a dense one.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do QR codes expire?
faq.a1: Static ones never do. The data is in the pattern itself, so a code printed today will still scan in twenty years if the ink survives. A dynamic code depends on the redirect behind it and stops working if that goes away.
faq.q2: Why did my code stop scanning after I changed the colours?
faq.a2: Almost always contrast. Scanners threshold the image into light and dark before they read anything, so two mid-tone colours become one. Keep the foreground dark, the background light, and pay attention to the warning under the colour fields.
faq.q3: Can I put my logo in the middle?
faq.a3: Yes, and doing so forces error correction to level H, which is what lets a scanner rebuild the modules the logo covers. Keep the logo modest and print a test — parity spent on your logo is parity that is no longer available for a scratch.
faq.q4: Is a Wi-Fi QR code safe to put on the wall?
faq.a4: It contains the password in plain text, so treat it exactly like writing the password on the wall. That is fine for a guest network and a bad idea for the one your file server is on.
faq.q5: PNG or SVG?
faq.a5: SVG for anything that will be printed or resized — it is vector, so it stays sharp at any size. PNG for places that will not take an SVG, such as some social platforms and older design tools.
faq.q6: What happens if I lose the edit link?
faq.a6: The code keeps working and keeps redirecting to wherever it last pointed, but nobody can change it again. The token is stored only as a hash, so this service cannot look it up or recover it. The recent-codes list in the browser you created it from keeps a copy, which is the practical answer for most people — save it elsewhere too if the code is going on something you cannot reprint.
faq.q7: Does this tool track the codes I make?
faq.a7: Static codes are never sent anywhere, so there is nothing to track. Dynamic codes store the destination, a count of scans and the time of the last one. No location, device, or visitor identity is recorded with them.

understanding.title: What a short link actually is
understanding.p1: A short link is not a copy of your address — it is a pointer to it. This tool stores your destination against a {length, number}-character code and hands you an address ending in that code; whoever follows it is sent on with an HTTP 302, so their browser asks this service where to go every single time.
understanding.example: /s/aB3xK9 → 302 → your destination — asked again on every visit, which is what makes the destination changeable
understanding.p2: A permanent redirect would be cached by every browser that followed it once, and re-pointing the link later would reach only people who had never used it. Every hop here is temporary, uncached, and marked so search engines neither index the link nor pass this site's ranking on to yours. Destinations may be up to {limit, number} characters and must be http or https — a short link that could carry any scheme would be a way to host an attack behind a name people trust.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Can I change where a short link points after sharing it?
faq.a1: Yes — that is the point of the edit link you get when the link is created. Open it, change the destination, and every copy of the short link already out there follows the new one immediately. The short link itself never changes.
faq.q2: What happens if I lose the edit link?
faq.a2: The link keeps working, but you cannot change it. Edit links are shown once and stored only as a digest, so nobody — including this service — can recover one. The recent-links list in your browser keeps a copy, which is the practical answer for most people.
faq.q3: Do short links expire on their own?
faq.a3: Only if you ask for it. Leave the schedule switch off and a link works until you change it. Turn it on and you can set when it starts working, when it stops, or both.
faq.q4: How safe is the password on a link?
faq.a4: It is stored as a salted PBKDF2 digest and the destination is never sent to the browser until the password is right. But there is no attempt limit beyond the cost of the hash, so treat it as a way to stop a link being casually opened rather than as protection for something genuinely sensitive.
faq.q5: Can I pick my own short name?
faq.a5: Yes. Turn on “Custom name” and type one — lowercase letters, numbers and single hyphens, three characters or more. If it is already taken, or reserved, you are told which so you can pick another rather than being handed something you did not ask for.
faq.q6: Is the list of my links stored on your server?
faq.a6: No. It lives in your browser's local storage and never leaves your machine. Open the tool in a different browser, or clear your site data, and the list is empty — though the links themselves keep working.
faq.q7: Do you track who clicks my links?
faq.a7: Only a count, and the time of the most recent visit. No per-visitor record is kept, the destination is sent no referrer, and nothing about the visitor reaches this service beyond the request itself.

understanding.title: What a slug actually is
understanding.p1: A slug is the readable part of a URL that names one page — the how-to-build-a-website in example.com/blog/how-to-build-a-website. It is not the title and it is not an id, but a short, stable label a reader and a crawler can both make sense of at a glance.
understanding.example: How to Build a Website! → how-to-build-a-website — spaces become the separator, the ! is dropped, and the case is folded
understanding.p2: Which makes a slug generator mostly a set of decisions rather than an algorithm: what joins the words, whether the accents survive, how long is too long. Only four marks pass through a URL untouched — -, _, . and ~ — so those are the separators on offer, and everything else RFC 3986 either reserves or percent-encodes, which is how a space becomes %20. Every character is transformed in this tab; nothing you type is uploaded.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Should I use a dash or an underscore?
faq.a1: A dash, unless you have a specific reason not to. Search engines have long read a hyphen as a word boundary and an underscore as part of a word, so learn-css reads as two words where learn_css can read as one. The difference is smaller than it once was, but the safer choice costs nothing.
faq.q2: Why does Next.js become next-js rather than nextjs?
faq.a2: Because the tool follows one rule: anything that is not a letter or a digit ends a word. The full stop in Next.js is a boundary like any other, so the two halves are joined by your separator. If you want nextjs, take the dot out of the heading first, or edit the result — this is a deliberate call rather than a guess about which dots are meaningful.
faq.q3: Can I use any character I like as a separator?
faq.a3: Only the four that RFC 3986 leaves unreserved: hyphen, underscore, full stop and tilde. Anything else — a space, a slash, an ampersand, a percent sign — either means something to a URL parser or is percent-encoded on the way out, which turns a readable slug into an unreadable one. Type one of those and the tool names the character and refuses, rather than quietly rewriting your choice.
faq.q4: What happens to a Bangla or Chinese heading?
faq.a4: With ASCII only switched on those letters have no ASCII form to fold to, so they are dropped — and if that leaves nothing at all, the tool says so instead of handing back an empty slug. Switch ASCII only off and the letters are kept exactly as typed, which every modern browser and host will accept.
faq.q5: How long should a slug be?
faq.a5: Short enough to read at a glance, long enough to say what the page is. Three to six words, or roughly 40 to 70 characters, covers most pages. The ceiling here cuts on a word boundary, so a capped slug still ends on a whole word.
faq.q6: Does any of this leave my browser?
faq.a6: No. Every character is transformed by JavaScript running in this tab. Nothing is uploaded, the page keeps no record of what you typed, and the tool works with the network disconnected.

understanding.title: What a case converter actually changes
understanding.p1: Case is the one thing about a piece of text that carries meaning without carrying words. HELP and help are the same four letters and two different tones of voice, and userName, user_name and User Name are the same two words wearing three different uniforms — a variable, a database column, and a label on a form.
understanding.example: ACCIDENTALLY LEFT THE CAPS LOCK ON → Accidentally left the caps lock on
understanding.p2: Retyping a paragraph to fix that is minutes of work, and retyping a heading as snake_case is minutes plus a typo. This tool does both in a keystroke, entirely inside your browser: nothing you paste is sent anywhere, and the conversion runs on the text as you type it.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does my text get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. Every case runs in your browser, on the text in the box, and the page makes no request while you type. You can turn off your connection and it keeps working.
faq.q2: What is the difference between Capitalized Case and Title Case?
faq.a2: Capitalized Case gives every word a capital. Title Case follows the convention headlines use: small words such as a, the, of and to stay lower case unless they open the line, close it, or follow a colon. So the art of the deal becomes The Art Of The Deal one way and The Art of the Deal the other.
faq.q3: Why did Sentence case turn my “I” into “i”?
faq.a3: Because it is one letter, and the acronym rule is “two capitals or more”. Deciding that a lone capital I is the English pronoun rather than a variable name, a grade or a Roman numeral would mean the tool guessing at your language, and guessing wrong on the text where it matters. Sentence case does the mechanical thing and leaves that one to you.
faq.q4: Can it convert a whole list in one go?
faq.a4: Yes — that is what “one line at a time” does, and it is on by default. Each line is converted on its own and the blank ones stay in place, so what comes back lines up row for row against what you pasted.
faq.q5: Why did an identifier case give me an error instead of a result?
faq.a5: Because there were no words in the text to build a name from. The identifier cases keep only letters and digits, so something like !!! ??? leaves nothing behind — and an empty box would look like a bug rather than an answer, so the tool says so instead.
faq.q6: How much text can I paste at once?
faq.a6: Up to {max} characters, which is a long chapter. Past that the tool refuses rather than freezing the tab, and the counter above the box starts warning you well before you reach it.

understanding.title: What a sorter has to get right
understanding.p1: Putting a list in order is one line of code, and nobody opens a web page for one line of code. The time goes on everything around it. Half the rows still carry the bullets they arrived with, three of them are blank, two say the same thing twice, and the paragraph in the middle came out of a PDF with a newline every sixty-six characters. Sort that as it stands and you get an alphabetised jumble with - in front of some of it and a sentence broken across three rows.
understanding.example: - cherry · - apple · - banana → 1. apple · 2. banana · 3. cherry
understanding.p2: So this page does the whole job in one pass: it works out where each item really ends, cleans the rows, orders them, and writes the markers back on afterwards — in that order, because any other one gets a different answer. All of it runs in this tab, and nothing you paste is sent anywhere.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.q1: Does any of this leave my browser?
faq.a1: No. The whole tool is a few pure functions running in this tab, and the page makes no request while you type. You can turn the network off and it will keep working.
faq.q2: Why does my list come back in a strange order for accented or non-Latin text?
faq.a2: Because the comparison is by Unicode code point rather than by any language's dictionary rules. That is a deliberate trade: reading collation data from the host would let the server and your browser disagree about the same list. It means ä sorts after z, and with case sensitivity on every capital comes before every lowercase letter.
faq.q3: Smart mode joined two lines that should have stayed apart. What now?
faq.a3: Switch the line-break control to Every line, which starts a new item at every newline and guesses nothing. It is worth checking the counter under the box first — it says how many lines were folded, so you can tell at a glance whether the mode is the problem.
faq.q4: Why is the sort key greyed out?
faq.a4: Because the order you picked does not compare anything. As typed, reverse and shuffle rearrange the rows without ever looking at what is in them, so there is no key for them to read. Choose ascending or descending and it comes back.
faq.q5: Will shuffling twice give the same list?
faq.a5: No — each press of the shuffle button draws a fresh arrangement. It is not a cryptographic shuffle and is not meant to be; for anything that has to be unguessable, use the password or secret generator instead.
faq.q6: How much can I paste at once?
faq.a6: Up to {maxCharacters} characters and {maxItems} lines, whichever it reaches first. Past either, the tool refuses rather than freezing the tab, and says which ceiling you met.

understanding.title: Why maths loses its shape in plain text
understanding.p1: Every superscript, fraction bar and integral sign in a piece of maths is carried by the layout rather than by the characters. Copy an equation out of a PDF, a chat message or a spreadsheet cell and the layout is exactly what gets dropped: a raised two becomes an ordinary digit, a fraction bar becomes a slash, and a summation sign becomes the word sum or nothing at all.
understanding.p2: This tool reads that flattened text back into LaTeX, and renders the result with KaTeX so you can check it. Both halves happen in your browser — the text is never sent anywhere — and the LaTeX stays editable, because a converter that guesses has to let you correct it.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does my equation get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The conversion and the rendering both run in your browser, and the page makes no request while you type. You can turn off your connection and it keeps working.
faq.q2: Can it read an equation from a screenshot?
faq.a2: Yes — switch the input to Image, then choose, drop or paste a PNG, JPEG or WebP. The picture goes to this site's server and on to a recognition model, is used once, and is not stored. That is the one path in this tool that leaves your browser, and the panel says so above the controls. Typing an equation instead sends nothing anywhere.
faq.q3: It read my subscript as a power. How do I fix it?
faq.a3: Because digits straight after a single letter are read as a power by default, which is right for x2 and wrong for H2O or a name like h264. Look under the source box: the other readings are already converted and previewed, so switching to the subscript or the as-typed version is one press. To skip the question entirely, write it outright in the input — H_2O for a subscript, a^2 for a superscript — and nothing is guessed at.
faq.q4: Will converting again lose my edits?
faq.a4: Yes, and the button says so before you press it. Everything below the input is replaced by a fresh conversion, including equations you have edited. Editing the LaTeX never triggers a conversion on its own — only the button does.
faq.q5: The preview shows an error. What now?
faq.a5: The message under the preview is KaTeX's own, and it names the command or the brace it stopped at. The most common cause is an unbalanced brace introduced while editing. Nothing about a broken equation affects the rest of the page.
faq.q6: Can I download the equation as an image?
faq.a6: Not at the moment. KaTeX renders to HTML and MathML rather than to a picture, so an SVG or PNG export would mean a second rendering engine and embedded font files — a much larger thing than it looks, and not something worth half-building. The MathML output is the closest thing on offer: a real vector-drawn equation in any browser that reads it.
faq.q7: How accurate is the image recognition?
faq.a7: Good enough to save you retyping, and not good enough to trust unread. It is a vision model transcribing symbols, so it can misread a subscript for a superscript, drop a bar, or guess wrong at a cramped exponent. Every equation it returns is marked as read from a picture, and the preview beside the source is there for exactly this — read the rendered equation before you use it.

howItWorks.title: What a diff actually computes
howItWorks.p1: Comparing two texts is not a matter of walking both from the top and reporting the first place they stop matching — insert one line at the start of a file and every line after it moves down by one. What a diff looks for instead is the longest sequence of lines the two texts still share, in order; everything in that sequence is unchanged, and everything else is an insertion or a deletion.
howItWorks.example: the quick brown fox vs the quick red fox → one changed row, with only brown and red tinted
howItWorks.p2: Two operations, then: insert and delete. A rewritten line is a deletion and an insertion that happen to land in the same place, so this tool pairs them back into one changed row and runs the same comparison again inside it, over words or characters — and that inner pass is the difference between reading a diff and hunting through one. Nothing here reaches the network, which is why a contract draft or a production config is as safe to paste as a code snippet.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.q1: Does anything I paste leave my browser?
faq.a1: No. The comparison, the highlighting and the patch are all computed in your browser, and the page has nothing to send them to. Uploading a file reads it locally too. You can put the page in a tab, disconnect, and it will keep working.
faq.q2: What does diff precision actually change?
faq.a2: Only what happens inside a line that already changed. At line precision the whole line is tinted. At word precision the comparison runs again over the words in it, so only the words that differ light up. At character precision it runs over single characters, which is what you want for a one-character difference and too noisy for a rewritten sentence. The set of changed lines is the same in all three.
faq.q3: I moved a block of lines and it says they were deleted and added. Why?
faq.a3: Because that is what a diff is: a list of insertions and deletions that turn one text into the other. A moved block is a deletion in one place and an insertion in another, and no ordering of those two operations describes it as a move. Some tools guess at moves afterwards; this one shows you the edit script, which is what a patch has to carry anyway.
faq.q4: Why is a line shown as unchanged when the two sides clearly differ?
faq.a4: An ignore option is on. Ignoring case or whitespace makes lines that differ only that way count as the same line — the row is marked and the count under the boxes says how many, so you can tell at a glance whether the match is real or the option's doing.
faq.q5: Will the patch apply cleanly with git?
faq.a5: Yes, provided the file you apply it to is the text you put in the left box. It is a standard unified diff with three lines of context, including the no-newline marker where a side needs one. Give it real filenames by renaming the download, or paste it wherever you would paste any patch.
faq.q6: Can I compare two files instead of pasting?
faq.a6: Yes — each side has an upload button that reads a text file into that box. It is read in your browser like everything else, so nothing is transferred, and the same size limits apply once the text is in.

howItWorks.title: How this compressor works
howItWorks.p1: Every file you drop is decoded to raw pixels, optionally scaled down, and handed to a WebAssembly build of a real production encoder — MozJPEG, libwebp, libaom or OxiPNG. These are the same codecs Squoosh ships.
howItWorks.example: canvas.toBlob → the browser's default JPEG writer, one quality knob, no way to ask for anything else
howItWorks.p2: That is the difference, and it is not marketing: a real encoder run slowly beats the one the browser hands you, which is why the settings are worth a look. All of it runs in this tab — no upload, no queue on somebody else's server, and no limit imposed by a plan; the ceiling is your own machine's memory, which is why the file count and megapixel caps exist.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is this better than compressing with an online service?
faq.a1: For output quality it is comparable — the encoders are the same ones most services run, at settings tuned past their defaults. For privacy it is not close: nothing is uploaded, so there is no copy on a server to be retained, indexed or leaked, and there is no per-day limit to hit.
faq.q2: Why did my file get bigger?
faq.a2: Because it was already compressed well. Re-encoding an image that was written at a high quality by a good encoder cannot find much left to remove, and the second encode adds its own overhead. When that happens the row shows a negative saving rather than hiding it, so you can keep the original.
faq.q3: Does compressing twice lose more quality?
faq.a3: Yes, for any lossy format. Each encode discards detail the previous one kept, and the losses accumulate — a JPEG re-saved five times looks visibly worse than the same image encoded once at the lowest of those five qualities. Always compress from the original, not from an earlier result.
faq.q4: Why is AVIF so much slower than the rest?
faq.a4: It is doing far more work. libaom searches many more ways of predicting each block than a JPEG or WebP encoder does, and that search is what buys the smaller file. Running it in WebAssembly costs a further factor on top. It is worth it for images you will serve many times, and rarely worth it for a one-off.
faq.q5: Can I compress an animated GIF?
faq.a5: Not as an animation. A GIF is decoded to its first frame and written back as a still image, so the animation is lost. Nothing here writes an animated format.
faq.q6: What happens to a transparent PNG if I choose JPEG?
faq.a6: It is composited onto white before encoding and the row tells you so. JPEG has no alpha channel, and the alternative — handing transparent pixels straight to the encoder — produces the black boxes you sometimes see where a logo used to be.

howItWorks.title: How the icons are drawn
howItWorks.p1: A favicon is the small picture a browser shows beside your page's title. This tool draws one from text — a letter, initials, a Bangla character or an emoji — at every size a browser, iOS and Android ask for, and packs them with a site.webmanifest and the tags that link them.
howItWorks.example: A on indigo, rounded → favicon.ico (16, 32, 48), favicon-96x96.png, apple-touch-icon.png, two manifest icons, site.webmanifest and head.html
howItWorks.p2: Every size is drawn from the text on its own rather than shrunk from a large one, so the 16-pixel tab icon stays sharp. The glyph is centred on its ink, not on its baseline — which is what keeps Bangla and emoji in the middle of the plate.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why is there no SVG favicon?
faq.a1: An SVG favicon would draw the text with whatever fonts the visitor's device has, because the font is not embedded in it. A letter set in this site's Inter would turn into the visitor's default sans-serif, and an emoji would change with every operating system. PNG and ICO hold the pixels themselves, so every visitor sees the icon you saw here.
faq.q2: Why does my emoji look different on another computer?
faq.a2: Emoji are drawn with your device's own emoji font, and Apple, Google, Microsoft and others each draw them differently. The pack holds exactly the icon in your preview; somebody making the same icon on another system gets that system's emoji.
faq.q3: What is a maskable icon?
faq.a3: Android launchers crop app icons to a circle, a squircle or a rounded square, depending on the device. A maskable icon fills its whole square with the background and keeps the glyph inside a central circle 80% of the edge across, which every mask is guaranteed to leave visible. It needs an opaque background, because the launcher fills the whole mask.
faq.q4: Why is the iOS icon square when I picked a circle?
faq.a4: iOS rounds a home-screen icon's corners itself. An icon that was already rounded or circular gets cut a second time, leaving a thin band of the wrong colour at each corner. The shape you pick applies to the tab icons and the manifest icons.
faq.q5: Where do the files go?
faq.a5: At the root of your site: browsers ask for /favicon.ico there even when nothing links to it. Then paste the contents of head.html into your page's head. The manifest's theme and background colours come from the background you picked, and are left out for a transparent icon.

howItWorks.title: How the conversion works
howItWorks.p1: Every file you drop is decoded to raw pixels in this tab, scaled if you asked for that, and handed to a real encoder compiled to WebAssembly — MozJPEG for JPG, libwebp for WebP, libaom for AVIF and OxiPNG for PNG. The SVG target is the exception, because it has no encoder at all: it writes outlines rather than pixels.
howItWorks.example: photo.png → photo.avif — the same pixels through libaom, not through canvas.toBlob
howItWorks.p2: These are the same encoders Squoosh runs, and they are why the output is not simply what the browser would have written. Nothing is uploaded: there is no server in this flow at all, the codecs are downloaded once on demand, and everything after that happens on your machine — so a picture converted here never leaves the tab it was dropped into.

faq.title: Questions people actually ask
faq.q1: Is this the same as the Image Compressor?
faq.a1: They share the same four encoders, and they answer different questions. The compressor's job is a smaller file — it will pick a format for you, or encode to all of them and keep the shortest result. This tool's job is a specific format you named, plus the two icon containers the compressor does not write at all. If you want a picture smaller, use the compressor; if you want it as AVIF or as a favicon, use this.
faq.q2: Which favicon files do I actually need?
faq.a2: If you only take one thing, take favicon.ico at your site root — browsers request it by path with no link tag at all. Everything else in the pack buys a specific improvement: the 96 for high-DPI tabs, the 180 for the iOS home screen, and the 192 and 512 with a manifest for the install prompt. Take the pack and delete what you do not want; adding one back later means regenerating it.
faq.q3: Why did my transparent logo come out with a white background?
faq.a3: Either you converted to JPG, which has no alpha channel and therefore has to put the picture on some colour, or the Background control was set to white. Set it to Keep transparent and convert to PNG, WebP or AVIF instead.
faq.q4: Can it convert HEIC, SVG or a RAW file?
faq.a4: SVG, yes — drop one in, pick any target, and it is drawn at the size you asked for rather than enlarged from a grid. HEIC and RAW, no: HEIC is only decodable in Safari, and RAW formats need a demosaicer that no browser ships. Convert those to PNG elsewhere first.
faq.q5: What happens to an animated GIF?
faq.a5: You get its first frame. Nothing here writes an animated format, so the other frames have nowhere to go — this is the one case where the conversion loses something the file extension will not warn you about.
faq.q6: Why is AVIF taking so long?
faq.a6: libaom is a slow encoder, and it is running in WebAssembly on one thread. That is the price of AVIF's size. On a large photograph, expect seconds rather than an instant; on a batch, expect to leave the tab open. WebP gets most of the saving for a fraction of the time.
faq.q7: Does converting a JPG to PNG make it better quality?
faq.a7: No, and this is worth being clear about. PNG is lossless, so it will preserve exactly what the JPG contained, artefacts included, usually in a much larger file. Detail lost in the original compression is gone; nothing can reconstruct it. Convert to PNG to stop further loss, not to undo loss already taken.
faq.q8: Why does my photograph look terrible as an SVG?
faq.a8: Because tracing is not a conversion, it is a re-drawing. A photograph has no flat regions to find, so the tracer invents thousands of small ones — the file is larger than the JPEG and worse to look at. Tracing is for pictures that were drawn: logos, icons, stencils, flat illustration. If you want a photograph smaller, convert it to AVIF or WebP instead.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.p1: The picture is decoded to raw pixels in your tab, and the crop is a row-by-row copy of the rectangle you dragged — no interpolation, no colour conversion, no rounding. Only after that is anything scaled, and only if the size you asked for differs from the crop’s own.
howItWorks.example: 4000 × 3000 → crop 1200 × 1200 → export 1200 × 1200 — the bytes are copied; ask for 600 × 600 instead and Lanczos3 runs
howItWorks.p2: So the step that can still cost you quality is the last one: writing those pixels as a JPEG re-compresses them however careful the crop was. Choose PNG and the crop comes back exactly as it went in. All of it happens here — nothing is uploaded unless you paste a picture’s address, and that field says so above the controls.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does cropping lose quality?
faq.a1: The crop itself does not — it copies the pixels you selected, byte for byte. What can lose quality is the step after it: scaling to a different size, and re-encoding to a lossy format. Ask for the crop’s own size and save as PNG and nothing is lost at all; the line under the buttons says which of the two will happen before you press Export.
faq.q2: How do I make a Bangladeshi passport photo?
faq.a2: Lock the crop to 45:55 or pick the Bangladesh passport preset, drag the box over the face, then export. The preset is 45 × 55 mm at 300 DPI, which is 531 × 650 pixels, and it writes 300 DPI into the file so a lab prints it at the right size. Choose JPG if the form asks for one.
faq.q3: Why is my print the wrong size when the pixels are right?
faq.a3: Because the file did not say what resolution it was for, so the program printing it guessed — usually 72 DPI, which comes out about four times too big for a 300 DPI photograph. Turn on "write the resolution into the file" and use PNG or JPEG; WebP and AVIF have nowhere to carry it.
faq.q4: Can I crop to a shape that is not on the list?
faq.a4: Yes. Choose Custom and type two numbers — 45:55, 16/9, or a single decimal like 1.78. The crop then keeps that shape however you drag it.
faq.q5: Can I paste a screenshot instead of saving it first?
faq.a5: Press Ctrl+V anywhere on the page. There is also a Paste button for browsers and devices where a paste event will not reach the page; that one asks for clipboard permission the first time, because the click is on our button rather than on the platform's paste.
faq.q6: What happens to a picture with a transparent background?
faq.a6: It keeps its transparency in PNG, WebP and AVIF. JPEG has no alpha channel at all, so anything transparent is flattened onto the background colour on the way in — which is why that colour stays live even when nothing is being padded.
faq.q7: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a7: Only if you paste a picture's address, and only that address. Everything else — the file you choose, the crop, the resize, the encode — happens in this tab.
faq.q8: Can I resize several pictures at once?
faq.a8: Yes. Pick or drop up to {count, number} at once; a paste or a fetched address adds one more each time. Every setting applies to all of them, the shape lock cuts each to the largest centred box of that shape, and Download all saves one ZIP. Cropping by hand, turning and mirroring are for one picture at a time, so remove the others to reach them.

whatItIs.title: What this does
whatItIs.p1: A background remover separates the subject of a photograph from everything behind it, and gives you back the subject on its own with a transparent edge. This one does it with an open segmentation model, ISNet, compiled to WebAssembly and run inside your browser tab.
whatItIs.example: a portrait on a busy street → the same portrait, alone, on a transparent background — then on white, or on a beach
whatItIs.p2: Your picture is never uploaded. The model's weights are, however, fetched from IMG.LY's CDN the first time you press the button — roughly a hundred megabytes, cached by your browser afterwards — and searching for a stock background asks Pexels through this server. Neither carries your photograph, and each is stated beside the control it belongs to: the download size on the quality picker, and what Pexels sees under the search field.

faq.title: Questions
faq.q1: Is my photo uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The segmentation runs in your browser tab through WebAssembly, and the composite is drawn on a canvas there too. The only network requests this page makes are for the model's weights and, if you use the Photo tab, for stock photographs — neither carries your picture.
faq.q2: Why is the first cut-out so slow?
faq.a2: The model has to be downloaded before it can run — between forty and a hundred and seventy megabytes depending on the quality you chose. Your browser caches it, so every cut-out after the first starts immediately.
faq.q3: Does this use an AI service or an API key?
faq.a3: No. It uses an open, published segmentation model that runs locally. There is no account, no key, no per-image cost and no request to any model provider.
faq.q4: Which quality should I pick?
faq.a4: Balanced, unless you have a reason. Drop to Fast on a slow connection or for a subject with a hard outline; go to Best when the edge is hair, fur or foliage and you can afford the download.
faq.q5: Can I do several pictures at once?
faq.a5: You can have five open at once and switch between them freely, but each is cut out on its own when you press the button for it. That is deliberate: each cut-out holds a full decoded bitmap in memory, and running five together is how a browser tab runs out of it.
faq.q6: Why can I not choose a background before removing it?
faq.a6: Because there is nothing to put a background behind until the subject has been cut out. The tabs unlock the moment the cut-out finishes, and after that changing a background is instant — it is a canvas redraw, not another run of the model.
faq.q7: Can I use the stock backgrounds commercially?
faq.a7: Yes. Pexels photographs are free for commercial use without permission or payment. Credit is not required but is asked for, and this page shows the photographer's name and a link beside your result. You may not redistribute the photographs as stock in their own right.
faq.q8: The edge around the hair is wrong. What can I do?
faq.a8: Try Best, which is meaningfully better on soft boundaries. Beyond that, a picture where the subject and the background are close in colour is genuinely hard for every model of this kind, and a manual mask in a full editor is the honest answer when the result has to be exact.

whatItIs.title: What a blur placeholder is for
whatItIs.p1: An image that has not loaded yet leaves a hole. Fill it with nothing and the text below jumps when the picture arrives; fill it with a grey box and the page looks broken rather than loading. A blur placeholder fills it with the picture's own colours, in roughly the right places, so the layout is settled before a single byte of the real file has arrived.
whatItIs.example: LEHV6nWB2yk8pyo0adR*.7kCMdnj — twenty-eight characters holding the low frequencies of a photograph, and nothing else
whatItIs.p2: That is short enough to sit in a database column beside the image's URL, to travel in the same JSON response as the rest of the record, and to be rendered from server-side markup with no extra request — which is the whole trick, because a placeholder that needs its own request arrives after the thing it was standing in for. This tool does both directions: give it a picture and it produces the hash, the base64 blurDataURL that next/image wants, and the snippet to use either one; give it a hash somebody else made and it paints it back.

faq.title: Questions people actually ask
faq.q1: Does this produce the same hash as blurha.sh?
faq.a1: Yes, character for character. This implementation follows the JavaScript reference implementation exactly, down to which rounding it uses and which order it sums the pixels in, and it is tested against that library across every combination of detail settings. A hash from here is read by react-blurhash, and by the Swift, Kotlin, Python and Rust ports, without qualification.
faq.q2: Why do I get a hash and a data URI rather than just one?
faq.a2: Because the two ecosystems want different things. react-blurhash and the mobile ports want the string and decode it themselves. next/image and plain CSS want a data URI and have never heard of BlurHash. Storing the hash and generating the data URI from it is the flexible answer; storing both is the fast one.
faq.q3: Should I store the hash or the blurDataURL in my database?
faq.a3: The hash, if you can. It is a quarter the length, it does not change when you decide the placeholder should be 48 pixels instead of 32, and you can always produce a data URI from it later. Store the data URI when the thing rendering it cannot run a decoder — a static export, an email, a template with no JavaScript.
faq.q4: Why is my transparent PNG's placeholder black behind the logo?
faq.a4: BlurHash has no alpha channel. Transparent pixels are read as whatever sits underneath them, which in a decoded canvas is black. Flatten the picture onto the background colour you actually use before generating the hash — the Image Converter on this site will do that — or use ThumbHash, which does carry alpha.
faq.q5: How long should the hash be?
faq.a5: Let the fit decide, which lands between forty-four and sixty characters depending on the shape. That is longer than the four-by-three, twenty-eight-character hash a lot of code ships, and it is deliberate: at twenty-eight characters a landscape photograph is a smudge with the right colours in roughly the right places, and the difference is plain when the two sit side by side. If storage genuinely matters, dial the pair down and watch the preview — two by two is a gradient, which is sometimes exactly right for a hero image.
faq.q6: Does the punch setting change what I store?
faq.a6: No. Punch is applied while painting, never while encoding, so the hash is identical at every punch value. What it does change is the PNG this page writes, because a PNG is pixels and has no coefficients left to scale — so if you are shipping the data URI, punch is baked in, and if you are shipping the hash, it is a prop your renderer sets.
faq.q7: Can I generate these on my server instead?
faq.a7: Yes, and for a real application you should — at upload time, once per picture, stored beside the URL. The blurhash package on npm does exactly what this page does, and there are equivalents for most languages. This tool is for the cases where you want to see one, check one, or produce a handful by hand.

whatItIs.title: What this actually builds
whatItIs.p1: Two things happen to your picture. First the subject is separated from its background, which gives an outline. Then that outline is inflated: every point is pushed out by how far inside the outline it sits, so the middle bulges and the edge closes, and the same bulge is mirrored behind — a rounded solid with a front, a back and a sealed edge. The picture's own light and shade is laid over the surface on top of that, so a face still reads as a face.
whatItIs.p2: It is worth being plain about what that is not. Nothing here knows what the back of your subject looks like, because a photograph does not say. What you get is the shape the outline implies, inflated — closer to a well-made soft toy of the thing than to the thing. For a logo, an icon, a leaf, a fish, a game asset, a fridge magnet or anything you are going to sculpt further, that is a real starting point and it prints. For an accurate model of a specific object you want photogrammetry from many angles or a scanner, and no amount of tuning here substitutes for one.
whatItIs.p3: The other two shapes do something different and older: they lay the picture on a flat plate or wrap it around a cylinder as relief, with no attempt at a body. That is what a lithophane, a plaque, an engraved sign or a lamp shade is, and it is why they are still here.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Will this turn a photo of an object into an accurate 3D model of that object?
faq.a1: Not accurate, no — nothing that reads a single photograph honestly can. It cuts the subject out, inflates its outline into a rounded solid and lays the picture's shading over it, which gets you the object's silhouette, proportions and surface pattern as a printable body. What it cannot get is the back, or anything hidden in the picture. For a logo, an icon, a game asset, a magnet or a base to sculpt on, that is genuinely useful. For an accurate replica you need photogrammetry from many angles or a scanner.
faq.q2: Which format should I download?
faq.a2: GLB unless you have a reason not to. It is one file, it carries the picture inside it, and everything modern opens it. Choose STL if it is going straight to a slicer, OBJ if something in your pipeline is old enough to want it, and PLY if you want per-vertex colour without a texture file.
faq.q3: Why is my GLB tiny in Blender?
faq.a3: Because it is correct. glTF measures in metres and has no way to say otherwise, so a 100 mm plate is 0.1 units. Select it, press S, type 1000 and press Enter. STL, OBJ and PLY are unitless and are written in millimetres, which is what every tool that reads them assumes.
faq.q4: How do I make a lithophane?
faq.a4: Switch Invert on, keep the solid backing on, set the backing thickness to the thinnest you want light to pass through, and keep the relief depth small — a millimetre or two of variation is usually plenty. Print it standing up at a fine layer height with solid walls. Test on a small strip first: the numbers depend on your filament far more than on this tool.
faq.q5: The model has a visible seam on the cylinder. Is it broken?
faq.a5: No. The mesh is closed there — the two edges are literally the same vertices — but the picture's left edge and right edge are different pixels, so the relief steps where they meet. It is the same seam you would get wrapping a photograph around a jar. Use a picture that tiles horizontally if you need it to disappear.
faq.q6: Is the model watertight enough to print?
faq.a6: With the solid backing on, yes. Every edge in the mesh is shared by exactly two triangles facing the same way, which is what manifold means, and it is checked by the test suite on both shapes rather than assumed. With the backing off you get the surface alone, which is deliberately not watertight — a slicer will complain, and it should.
faq.q7: Does my picture get uploaded?
faq.a7: No. Decoding, sampling, meshing and writing the file all happen in this tab. The only thing that ever leaves is the optional field that fetches a picture from a URL for you, which has to go through the server because of how browsers handle cross-origin images — and that is a picture going in, never a model coming out.
faq.q8: Does the cut-out send my picture anywhere?
faq.a8: No. The model runs in your browser — what travels is the model coming to your machine, not your picture leaving it. Its weights are fetched once from a CDN, the size is written on the control, and your browser caches them: the second picture costs nothing, and so does the Background Remover, which uses the same file. If you have already fetched a heavier tier there, this tool starts on it rather than downloading a lighter one.
faq.q9: Part of my model is paper-thin. Why?
faq.a9: The outline is carried on the same grid as the mesh, so anything narrower than one sample has no inside for the inflation to find, and the front and back meet there instead of enclosing anything. Raise the resolution — a thin neck that pinches at 96 samples is usually solid by 192. It is sealed either way, so it will still slice.
faq.q10: How does it know what is near and what is far?
faq.a10: It estimates. A monocular depth model — Depth Anything V2, small — runs in your browser and reads the picture as a scene, the way you do: a nose is in front of a face, a chest in front of shoulders. That estimate becomes the relief on the surface. It is a guess about relative depth over the front of the subject, good enough for a face to read as a face, and it says nothing about the back — no picture does.

what.title: What this answers
what.p1: A domain is several independent systems wearing one name. A registry knows who registered it and when it lapses. Its nameservers know what it resolves to. The network it resolves into belongs to somebody else again. And the machine at the far end presents a certificate, sends headers, and serves a page built out of software with its own licences.
what.example: an expiry date beside a certificate date, a nameserver beside the CDN it points at, an SPF record beside the MX records it is supposed to cover
what.p2: Asking each of them separately is four tools and a terminal; this asks all of them at once and puts the answers side by side, which is usually where the interesting part is. Nothing here is privileged information — every answer comes from a service that publishes it deliberately: the DNS, the registry, the routing registries, and the site's own responses.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is this WHOIS?
faq.a1: It is RDAP, which is what replaced WHOIS. The same data, published as JSON over HTTPS instead of as free text on port 43 — which is why the fields here are read rather than guessed at out of prose. Every gTLD is required to run one; a few country registries still do not, and those are reported as such.
faq.q2: Why is the registration panel empty for my .de domain?
faq.a2: Because that registry publishes no RDAP service, so there is nothing to query. The panel says so instead of showing a blank record, and the registry's own WHOIS page has the answer.
faq.q3: Why is the registrant's name hidden?
faq.a3: Since GDPR came into force in 2018, gTLD registries have redacted personal data from public records. The registrar, the dates, the status codes and an abuse contact stay public; the person does not.
faq.q4: The technologies panel found nothing — is the site hiding?
faq.a4: Possibly, and possibly it is just quiet. A CDN configured to strip identifying headers, a page rendered entirely by script after load, and a stack with no fingerprint of its own all look identical from outside. Absence of evidence is the honest reading.
faq.q5: Can I look up an IP address?
faq.a5: Yes. The name breakdown, hosting, certificate and HTTP panels all work. Forward DNS and domain registration do not apply to an address and say so. Private and reserved addresses are refused.
faq.q6: Does the site I inspect know about it?
faq.a6: If the site fetch is on, yes: it receives one GET request for its home page from our server, identified as ToolForgeBot. Turn the switch off and only the resolver and the registry are contacted.
faq.q7: Why is there a challenge on a read-only lookup?
faq.a7: Because the alternative is a public endpoint that fetches whatever host anyone names, from our address. Without the challenge it would be somebody's free scanner within a day, and the complaints would arrive here.
faq.q8: The propagation card says resolvers disagree. Is my DNS broken?
faq.a8: Not necessarily. Two ordinary things produce that result. The first is a change still spreading: until the previous record’s TTL expires, resolvers that cached it keep serving it, and the TTL shown beside each answer is how long that can last. The second is GeoDNS steering, where the name is configured to return different addresses depending on where the question came from, which is how many large sites route visitors to a nearby server. If you have not changed anything recently, the second is the likely explanation.

understanding.title: Three notations, one data model
understanding.p1: BSON, JSON and TOON all describe the same thing: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. They agree about almost nothing else — BSON is binary, length-prefixed and typed, JSON is text with exactly six types, and TOON trades JSON's punctuation for indentation and a CSV-style table so a document costs fewer tokens in an LLM prompt.
understanding.example: '{'"_id": '{'"$oid": "6a69eb40a1b2c3d4e5f60718"'}''}' — Extended JSON is how an ObjectId survives a format that only knows strings and numbers
understanding.p2: So this tool never rewrites one notation into another. It reads whichever you paste into one plain value and writes that value out in whichever you asked for, which is why BSON → TOON cannot develop its own opinion about what a date is. Where the model runs out is BSON's type system — it knows an ObjectId from a string and an int32 from a double — and the bridge is Extended JSON, which travels through TOON unchanged. Nothing is uploaded: reading, writing and export all happen in this tab.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does this upload my document anywhere?
faq.a1: No. Every conversion runs in this tab and the page has no server behind it. That includes the file you open and the file you download.
faq.q2: What is the difference between canonical and relaxed Extended JSON?
faq.a2: Canonical writes every value in a wrapper naming its BSON type, so the document returns as the exact bytes it came from. Relaxed writes plain values wherever plain JSON can hold them, which reads better but loses the distinction between a double and an integer, and loses precision past ±2⁵³. After a relaxed read this tool checks your own document and tells you which of the two happened.
faq.q3: Is TOON always smaller than JSON?
faq.a3: No. It wins on uniform arrays of objects, where the field list is written once instead of on every row — often by half against indented JSON. On a deeply nested document with no repetition it lands near minified JSON and sometimes slightly above it. The counts under the output tell you which, for the document in front of you.
faq.q4: Can I convert a .bson file from mongodump?
faq.a4: One document at a time. mongodump writes a stream of documents back to back and this tool reads a single document, so opening such a file loads its bytes but the conversion stops at the length check once the first document ends.
faq.q5: Why does my ObjectId come out as a $oid object?
faq.a5: Because JSON has no ObjectId. That wrapper is Extended JSON, which is what mongosh prints, what mongoexport writes and what mongoimport reads — so it is not a lossy fallback, it is the interchange format. Feed it back in and the ObjectId returns.
faq.q6: Which version of TOON does this write?
faq.a6: TOON 4.1, through the format's own reference implementation rather than a re-reading of the specification — so what comes out of here is what every other TOON reader expects to see.
faq.q7: Why does the tool count characters instead of tokens?
faq.a7: Because a token count is a property of a model, not of a document. Two tokenizers disagree, and shipping one would mean shipping a megabyte of vocabulary to answer for a single model. Characters are exact, and the ratio between two formats holds directionally whichever tokenizer reads them.

understanding.title: What a connect scan actually tells you
understanding.p1: A TCP port is not a door that is open or shut. It is a number a program may have asked the operating system to listen on, and the only way to find out from outside is to try to start a conversation and see what comes back. This tool opens a real TCP connection to each port, watches the three-way handshake, and closes it again without writing or reading a single byte.
understanding.example: handshake completes → open; the host resets → closed; nothing comes back before the deadline → filtered
understanding.p2: The difference between the last two is the part most hosted port checkers throw away, and reporting a timeout as closed is a false statement about the network: closed proves a live host declined, while filtered proves nothing about the port and quite a lot about the firewall in front of it. If every port on a scan comes back filtered, the useful conclusion is that nothing answered — not that the host is secure.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does the host I scan see my IP address?
faq.a1: No, it sees ours. A page in a browser cannot open a raw TCP socket, so the scan has to run on a server, and the connection comes from this site's address. That is a property of every hosted port checker, not just this one — and it is why the tool is rate limited and why the copy asks you to scan hosts you are authorised to test.
faq.q2: Why is a port reported as filtered rather than closed?
faq.a2: Because nothing came back. Closed means the host actively refused — it sent a TCP reset, which took a reachable machine to send. Filtered means the probe vanished: a firewall dropped it without replying, or the host is not there at all. They are different facts, and folding them together is a lie a lot of port checkers tell.
faq.q3: Can I scan an internal address like 192.168.1.1?
faq.a3: No. Private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, cloud metadata and reserved ranges are all refused, including an IPv4 address disguised inside an IPv6 literal. The scan would run from our network rather than yours, so it would tell you nothing about your LAN and would turn this tool into a way through our own firewall. For an internal scan, run nmap on a machine inside that network.
faq.q4: Why only a few scans an hour?
faq.a4: Because the scan carries our address, an unmetered scanner is an anonymous scanning service, and the first thing that happens to one of those is that the networks worth scanning stop accepting traffic from it. The count is kept against a salted hash of your address in a database rather than in memory, because a limit that resets when a serverless instance recycles is not a limit.
faq.q5: Why does the service column say SSH when I am running something else there?
faq.a5: Because it is a static table of what each port is registered for, not a reading of what answered. Nothing here reads the banner a service announces or probes for a version — that is fingerprinting, it doubles the time per open port, and it is a meaningful step from "is this reachable" toward reconnaissance. The column tells you what the port is conventionally for; the state tells you what is true.
faq.q6: Can it scan UDP?
faq.a6: No, TCP only. UDP has no handshake, so there is nothing to observe: an open UDP port and a filtered one both usually answer with silence, and telling them apart means sending protocol-specific payloads and waiting far longer per port. A UDP scan that reported anything useful here would be guessing.
faq.q7: Is it legal to scan a host I do not own?
faq.a7: It depends where you are, where the host is, and what you agreed to — and in several jurisdictions the answer is no. Unauthorised probing falls under computer misuse law in the UK, the US and elsewhere. Scan your own hosts, or ones you have written permission to test. This is not legal advice.

understanding.title: What a subdomain lookup can actually see
understanding.p1: There is no query that asks a domain for its subdomains. DNS answers questions about names you already know: ask for the address of api.example.com and you get one, ask what names exist under example.com and there is no such question to ask. Zone transfers used to answer it and are refused by every nameserver worth running.
understanding.p2: So every subdomain finder works the same way: it collects names that were published somewhere else and indexes them. The largest such source is certificate transparency — since 2018, browsers reject a certificate that was not logged in a public append-only log, and every certificate carries the hostnames it covers. A staging box that was given HTTPS is a hostname in a public log, permanently.
understanding.example: example.com → api.example.com, staging.example.com, vpn.example.com …
understanding.p3: That is the trade this tool makes. It is passive: nothing is probed, no DNS request is made on your behalf, and the domain you name is never contacted. What comes back is what was published, which is not the same as what exists.

faq.title: Questions
faq.q1: Is this the same as crt.sh?
faq.a1: It draws on the same certificate transparency logs, but crt.sh is a searchable database of whole certificates while the index behind this tool keeps only three fields per name: the domain, the name, and when it was first seen. That is why it can answer a domain-wide query quickly, and why it cannot tell you which certificate a name came from.
faq.q2: Does this touch the domain I type?
faq.a2: No. The lookup is entirely passive: one request to the index, and nothing to the domain itself. No DNS query is made on your behalf, no port is opened, and the domain's own logs will show nothing.
faq.q3: Why are some names missing?
faq.a3: Because they were never published anywhere the index reads. A subdomain that has only ever had a private or self-signed certificate, that is not in a crawl, and that does not appear in a zone file leaves no public trace. A wildcard certificate is the common case: *.example.com covers every name under it and publishes none of them.
faq.q4: Why do some names have no date?
faq.a4: The index draws on sources that carry no timestamp, such as blocklists and some crawl data. Those names are listed with an unknown date rather than being given an invented one, and they sort last under both date orders.
faq.q5: A name is listed but does not resolve. Is the tool wrong?
faq.a5: No — that is the tool working as designed. The index records that a name was published, and never deletes it. A decommissioned host stays in the list forever, which is a large part of the value: those are exactly the names worth checking.
faq.q6: Why was my domain widened to something shorter?
faq.a6: The index is keyed by registrable domain, so it can only be asked about an eTLD+1. Type api.staging.example.co.uk and the lookup runs on example.co.uk, which returns a superset of what you asked for — every name under api.staging is in that answer. The result says what it did rather than answering a different question silently.
faq.q7: Can I look up any domain, or only my own?
faq.a7: Anything the index holds, because all of it is already public — the data comes from logs, zone files and crawls that anyone can read. That is the difference between this and the port scanner: nothing here touches somebody else's machine. What you do with the list is a different question, and the usual rule applies — test only what you own or have written permission to test.
faq.q8: What happens with a domain that has thousands of names?
faq.a8: The table pages at a hundred rows, while the filter, the ordering, the counts and every download work over the whole result. Past twenty thousand names the tool keeps the first twenty thousand and says so rather than pretending the list is complete. The very largest domains are refused by the index itself with a message saying so.

understanding.title: What this tool actually shows you
understanding.p1: Give it an address, a list of hosts, or the output of a traceroute you already ran, and it looks up who was allocated each address and where that allocation was registered. The globe is the answer drawn; the table beside it is the same answer written down, and it always holds more than the globe can.
understanding.p2: It cannot run a traceroute for you. Tracing a path needs raw sockets and sends packets to every machine along it, and a web page that did that on demand would be a free, anonymous probing service pointed at whoever you named. So run traceroute, tracert or mtr on your own machine, paste what it printed, and this maps it.
understanding.example: traceroute example.com | pbcopy — then paste it here.
understanding.p3: Everything it queries is public and readable by anyone: DNS over HTTPS, Team Cymru's ASN zones, and the RDAP bootstrap. No packet from this tool reaches the hosts on your map.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.q1: Does this run a traceroute for me?
faq.a1: No, and it will not. Tracing a path sends packets to every machine along it, and a web page doing that on demand for anonymous visitors is a probing service. Run the trace yourself and paste what it printed.
faq.q2: Why is the dot in the middle of the country instead of on the city?
faq.a2: Because that is the resolution of the evidence. The country comes from the routing registry's record of who was allocated the block, and a registry records a country, not a street. A city-level pin would be a geo-IP guess dressed up as a fact.
faq.q3: Why do several hops share one dot?
faq.a3: They were allocated to the same country, so they have the same coordinate. The globe groups them into one larger dot by default rather than stacking them invisibly, and the table lists every hop separately.
faq.q4: Why does a hop say it has no country?
faq.a4: The address was found and the network was named, but no registry stated which country the block was allocated to. It happens with older allocations and with some transit networks. The hop is real — there is simply nowhere honest to draw it.
faq.q5: Does my traceroute output leave my browser?
faq.a5: The addresses and names in it do. They are sent to our server, which queries public DNS, Team Cymru and the RDAP registries on your behalf. Those upstreams see our address, not yours. Nothing about the route is stored; the only record kept is a count against a hash of your address, so the hourly limit can be enforced.
faq.q6: Why is my first hop a private address?
faq.a6: Because it is your own router. Addresses in the private ranges belong to no registry and are the same numbers on millions of networks, so there is nothing to look up and nowhere to put them on a globe.
faq.q7: Can I use this from a script or an assistant?
faq.a7: Yes. The same lookup is exposed over MCP as a tool that returns every hop as data, coordinates included, with the same hourly limit applied.

understanding.title: What this page shows you
understanding.p1: Every request your browser makes carries a return address, and this page shows the one it arrived from. That is your public IP: the address of your router, your mobile carrier's gateway or your VPN, not the private one your device has on the local network.
understanding.example: curl https://…/api/ip → 203.0.113.7 — add ?format=json for the headers too
understanding.p2: The network panel names who announces the address — the ASN, operator, prefix and the country its block was allocated to — from reverse DNS and Team Cymru's routing data. That is a registry record, not a guess at your city, so it names your provider's country rather than your street.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.q1: Why is this different from the IP address in my network settings?
faq.a1: Your device usually has a private address such as 192.168.1.20 that only your local network can see. Your router swaps it for one shared public address on the way out, and that public address is the one every website sees — and the one shown here.
faq.q2: Why do I see an IPv6 address and not IPv4, or the other way round?
faq.a2: A connection uses one family at a time. If your network has IPv6, your browser normally prefers it, so that is what arrives. You may have an IPv4 address as well; this page can only see the one your browser chose for this request.
faq.q3: Why is the location only a country?
faq.a3: Because that is what the routing registry records about an address block. A city-level pin would come from a geo-IP database's guess, which is often wrong for mobile networks and VPNs. On a VPN you will see the VPN's exit address and its network instead of yours.
faq.q4: How do I get my IP from a script?
faq.a4: Run curl against /api/ip for the address alone, followed by a newline, or add ?format=json for the address and the headers as JSON. Neither does any lookup, so polling it is cheap.
faq.q5: Does this page store my IP address?
faq.a5: This tool saves nothing. It reads the address from your request and looks up the network through public DNS, which sees this server's address, not yours. Like any website, the hosting platform keeps its ordinary request logs.
