understanding.title: How a Unix mode is written
understanding.p1: Every file on Linux, macOS and the BSDs carries twelve permission bits: read, write and execute for its owner, its group and everyone else, plus three special bits. chmod sets them, and ls -l prints them back as letters.
understanding.example: 755 → rwxr-xr-x → u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx — the owner gets 4 + 2 + 1, the group and others 4 + 1
understanding.p2: Each octal digit is one audience, and the digit is the sum of read 4, write 2 and execute 1; a fourth digit in front holds setuid, setgid and sticky the same way. Every string this page writes was checked against GNU chmod and stat for all 4,096 modes, and all of it happens in this tab.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: What does a fourth digit in front of the mode do?
faq.a1: It holds the three special bits, weighted like the others: 4 is set-user-ID, 2 set-group-ID, 1 sticky. 4755 is 755 plus set-user-ID, which ls -l shows as rwsr-xr-x. A leading 0, as in 0755, means none of them.
faq.q2: What does a capital S or T mean?
faq.a2: The special bit is set but execute is not. A lowercase s or t means both are. On a file, a set-ID bit without execute does nothing, so a capital S usually means execute was removed by accident.
faq.q3: Why does chmod 755 leave set-group-ID on my directory?
faq.a3: GNU chmod keeps a directory's set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits unless you name them, and that holds for u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx as much as for 755. Clear them with chmod g-s dir or chmod u-s dir, or with an extra leading zero: chmod 00755 dir. On a regular file, both forms set exactly the mode shown.
faq.q4: Is 777 ever the right answer?
faq.a4: Rarely. It lets every account on the machine — and every process running as one, such as a compromised web server — change or replace the file. When two people need to write, put them in one group and use 775 or 664. The exception is a shared scratch directory such as /tmp, which is 1777: the sticky bit stops people deleting each other's files.
faq.q5: Can I type u+x or work out a umask here?
faq.a5: No — this page sets whole modes only. u+x changes whatever mode a file already has, so its result depends on a file this page cannot see, and a umask is taken away from the mode a program asks for when it creates one. The assignment form, u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx, is the symbolic way to state the whole mode.
faq.q6: Can I paste a line from ls -l?
faq.a6: Paste its first column. drwxr-sr-x works, file-type letter and all, and so does the trailing ., + or @ that SELinux, ACLs and macOS extended attributes add. Case matters, because s and S are different modes.

understanding.title: Why Bijoy text has to be converted at all
understanding.p1: For two decades most Bangla typed in Bangladesh was typed in Bijoy, and what it left behind is not Bangla to a computer. A SutonnyMJ font draws Bangla shapes in the slots an ordinary font keeps for Latin letters, so the file underneath says Avgvi †mvbvi evsjv and only that font turns it into আমার সোনার বাংলা. Paste it into a browser, a phone or a search box and the Latin letters are all anybody sees.
understanding.example: Avgvi †mvbvi evsjv → আমার সোনার বাংলা
understanding.p2: Converting it takes more than swapping letters. Bijoy stores text in the order it is drawn, so the ি of কি comes before the ক, and a reph comes after the letter it sits on. This tool reads each code as the glyph it draws, puts the vowel signs and rephs back in the order the language is spoken, and does it all inside your browser: nothing you paste is uploaded.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does my text get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. Both directions run in your browser, on the text in the box, and the page makes no request while you type. It keeps working with your connection turned off.
faq.q2: Which fonts does it work with?
faq.a2: SutonnyMJ, and the other Bijoy fonts whose names end in MJ, which share its layout. Older legacy fonts that put the Bangla glyphs in places of their own are a different encoding, and their text will not come out right here.
faq.q3: Why does the Unicode → Bijoy result look like Latin letters?
faq.a3: Because that is what Bijoy is. The result reads as Bangla only once it is set in SutonnyMJ or another Bijoy font: paste it into your document, select it, and change the font. Any English in the same passage turns into Bangla shapes too, because Bijoy cannot tell the two apart, so set those words back in an ordinary font afterwards.
faq.q4: What happens to English words and numbers in a Bijoy document?
faq.a4: They are read as Bijoy as well. In a Bijoy file an English word and a Bangla one are the same Latin letters, and only the font they were set in told them apart — which the pasted text no longer carries. Digits become Bangla numerals for the same reason. If your document mixed in English set in an ordinary font, convert the Bangla passages on their own, or retype the English afterwards.
faq.q5: A few symbols came out wrong. Why?
faq.a5: Some Bijoy codes mean two things. ’ is ্থ after a half-letter and a closing quote anywhere else; © is a reph after a letter and a copyright sign on its own; ° is ক্ক in a word and a degree sign after a number. The tool decides from the characters around each one, which is right in ordinary text and can be wrong where Bangla runs straight into a symbol. Fix the odd one by hand.
faq.q6: How much text can I convert at once?
faq.a6: Up to {max} characters — a whole document pasted from Word. Past that the tool refuses rather than freezing the tab, and the counter above the box starts warning you well before you reach it.

understanding.title: Writing a number the way a cheque needs it
understanding.p1: A number in words is the version nobody can quietly change, which is why a cheque, a deed or an invoice spells the amount out beneath the digits. In Bangladesh it often has to be right twice: 12,50,500 is twelve lakh fifty thousand five hundred in English and বারো লক্ষ পঞ্চাশ হাজার পাঁচ শত in Bangla, and both can go on the same form.
understanding.example: 12,50,500.75 → twelve lakh fifty thousand five hundred taka and seventy-five paisa only
understanding.p2: Bangla is the harder half. Every number below a hundred has a word of its own — twenty-one is একুশ, not বিশ এক — so there is no rule to fall back on, only a table that has to be right. This tool writes both lines at once, counts in lakhs and crores or in millions, and does it all inside your browser.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is the number sent anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The words are worked out in your browser as you type, and the page makes no request while you do. It keeps working with your connection turned off.
faq.q2: What is the difference between Number and Amount?
faq.a2: Number reads the value itself, so 10.5 is ten point five. Amount reads it as money, so the same 10.5 is ten taka and fifty paisa — the decimals are hundredths rather than digits — and the line ends in “only”, as a cheque's does.
faq.q3: How are numbers above a crore written?
faq.a3: On the South Asian ladder every step after the thousand is a hundred times the last: lakh, crore, then arab (ten to the ninth), kharab, neel, padma and shankh (ten to the seventeenth). Past a shankh the count of shankhs is itself a number, so ten to the nineteenth is one hundred shankh. The Bangla line always counts this way — আরব, খরব, নীল, পদ্ম, শঙ্খ — and the English line does too when it is set to lakhs and crores.
faq.q4: Why শত and লক্ষ rather than শো and লাখ?
faq.a4: Because a number in words is usually going onto something formal, and the written register uses শত and লক্ষ: এক লক্ষ পঁচিশ হাজার পাঁচ শত. শো and লাখ are what people say aloud, and both are good Bangla — they are just not what a cheque or a deed is written in.
faq.q5: Why was an amount with three decimals refused?
faq.a5: Because taka, rupees, dollars, euros and pounds all divide into a hundred, so a third decimal is not something anybody can pay. Rounding it would put a sum on the cheque that nobody wrote down, so the tool asks you to decide instead.
faq.q6: How large a number can it read?
faq.a6: Up to {digits} digits before the decimal point — 999 duotrigintillion on the international scale, past a googol — and {decimals} after it. Exactly ten to the hundredth reads as one googol. It stops there because that is where the standard English names run out.

understanding.title: Why one plot of land has five different sizes
understanding.p1: A plot in Bangladesh is bought in কাঠা, recorded in শতাংশ, surveyed in square feet and taxed in acres, so the same piece of ground needs several answers at once. The standard ones are fixed: a কাঠা is 720 sq ft, a বিঘা is 20 কাঠা, a শতাংশ is a hundredth of an acre, and a গণ্ডা in the land record is 864 sq ft, twenty of them to a কানি.
understanding.p2: The trouble starts outside Dhaka. A বিঘা is 52 শতাংশ in Faridpur and 60 in Rangpur, and a কানি is 120 শতাংশ in Comilla and Noakhali, against the standard 40. This converter uses the government's sizes unless you choose a district, says beside every figure which size it used, and draws the plot next to something you have stood beside — a bed, a parking space, a badminton or tennis court, a football pitch — so you can see how much land the number actually is.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is anything I type sent anywhere?
faq.a1: No. Every figure is worked out in your browser as you type, and the page makes no request while you do. It keeps working with your connection turned off.
faq.q2: Which sizes does it use by default?
faq.a2: The government's: a কাঠা of 720 sq ft and 16 ছটাক, a বিঘা of 20 কাঠা (33.06 শতাংশ), a শতাংশ of 435.6 sq ft, an অযুতাংশ of a hundredth of a শতাংশ, a গণ্ডা of 864 sq ft, a কানি of 20 গণ্ডা, a কড়া of a quarter গণ্ডা, a ক্রান্তি of a third of a কড়া, a তিল of a twentieth of a ক্রান্তি, and a বর্গহাত of 1.5 × 1.5 ft.
faq.q3: Why is a বিঘা different in my district?
faq.a3: Because the বিঘা and the কানি were local measures long before there was a national one, and many districts kept their own. The district sizes here come from Banglapedia's agrometrology tables. Choosing one changes the units under it too — a Faridpur কাঠা is a twentieth of a Faridpur বিঘা — and leaves the শতাংশ, acre and square feet alone, because those are defined the same everywhere. If your deed names a different size, the deed is right.
faq.q4: Is a গণ্ডা 2 শতাংশ or 864 sq ft?
faq.a4: The land record says both, and they are not quite the same: 2 শতাংশ is 871.2 sq ft. This tool uses 864 sq ft, because the units under the গণ্ডা — কড়া 216, ক্রান্তি 72, তিল 3.6 — are all written in square feet, and keeping them whole keeps the chain consistent. That makes the standard কানি 39.67 শতাংশ rather than exactly 40.
faq.q5: What does the size picture compare my land with?
faq.a5: The largest everyday thing your land is at least as big as, drawn beside it at the same scale: a single bed (1.9 × 0.9 m), a car parking space (5 × 2.5 m), a badminton court (13.4 × 6.1 m), a tennis court (23.77 × 10.97 m), a futsal court (40 × 20 m) or a football pitch (105 × 68 m). So five কাঠা reads as about 1.3 tennis courts rather than a speck on a pitch. Land of a pitch or more is laid out on pitches, up to thirty of them, after which the count says the rest.
faq.q6: How accurate are the figures?
faq.a6: Exact wherever the units are defined exactly — a foot is exactly 0.3048 m and an acre exactly 43,560 sq ft — and shown to four decimal places, or four significant digits for anything smaller than one. The figure you typed is always shown exactly as you typed it, never as a rounded round trip.

understanding.title: Counting an age the way a circular does
understanding.p1: A Bangladeshi job circular rarely asks how old you are. It asks how old you were on one date, the cut-off, and turns away anyone a single day outside its limit. The figure it wants is completed years, months and days, and the arithmetic is easy to get wrong by hand at the end of a month.
understanding.example: 12/05/1998 on 31/12/2026 → 28 years, 7 months, 19 days · born on a Tuesday, ২৯ বৈশাখ ১৪০৫ বঙ্গাব্দ
understanding.p2: Every date is also named in the Bangla calendar under the rule in force on it: Bangla Academy's 2019 revision from 1426 BS, which put 21 February back on ৮ ফাল্গুন and 16 December on ১ পৌষ, and the 1987 calendar before that — so a birth date reads the way a certificate of the time does. The page asks the server for today's date once, and everything else is worked out in your browser.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is the 30th birthday still inside “at most 30”?
faq.a1: Yes. A maximum of 30 runs up to 30 years, 0 months and 0 days on the cut-off date, so the 30th birthday itself is inside it and the day after is not. The result names the earliest date of birth that passes, so you can hold your certificate against one date instead of the arithmetic.
faq.q2: How does the COVID-19 age relaxation work?
faq.a2: The 2020 notices let circulars count the maximum age as of 25 March 2020 as well as on their own date, because recruitment stopped during the lockdown. Enter that date as the relaxation date — the button fills it in — and you pass the maximum if you were inside it on either date. The minimum is still counted on the circular's own date. Whether a relaxation applies, and to which posts, is decided notice by notice; BCS was excluded, so read the circular itself.
faq.q3: Why does a birth date in 2000 show a different Bangla day here?
faq.a3: Because it is converted under the calendar in force in 2000. From 1987 to 2019 Bangladesh's calendar gave বৈশাখ to ভাদ্র 31 days and ফাল্গুন 30, so 16 December 2000 was ২ পৌষ ১৪০৭. The 2019 revision made আশ্বিন 31 days and ফাল্গুন 29, which moves the same day to ১ পৌষ. Most converters apply the new rule to every year; a certificate issued at the time used the old one.
faq.q4: What about dates before 1987?
faq.a4: Bangladesh fixed its calendar in 1394 BS, on 14 April 1987. Before that the months followed the almanac (panjika), which set them astronomically, so no rule reproduces them exactly. The 1987 month lengths are applied backwards and those dates are marked; the almanac of the time may differ by a day. West Bengal's calendar is a different, astronomical one, and is not what this converts.
faq.q5: Why can the Hijri date be a day off?
faq.a5: The Hijri date here is the tabular Islamic calendar — arithmetic, and the same on every device. In Bangladesh each month begins when the new moon is sighted, as the Islamic Foundation announces, which can land a day or two either side. If the date you were told differs, shift it under Options; the shift applies to every date the tool names, in both directions.
faq.q6: How is somebody born on 29 February or the 31st counted?
faq.a6: By subtracting the fields and borrowing a month when the day comes out negative — the method taught by hand, and the one java.time uses. Somebody born on 29 February is 11 months 30 days old on 28 February of a common year and a year older on 1 March, which is also the day their birthday counts as for an age limit. Somebody born on 31 January is 1 month 1 day old on 1 March.
faq.q7: Whose “today” is today?
faq.a7: Bangladesh's. The page works out today's date in Dhaka when it loads, so a reader abroad late at night still gets the date the circular's office counts in.

understanding.title: What a photo says about you
understanding.p1: A phone writes far more into a photo than the picture. Alongside the pixels sit the GPS coordinates of where you stood, the exact second it was taken, the make, model and often the serial number of the camera, the software that edited it — and sometimes a thumbnail of the original that survives cropping. Most of it is invisible in a photo viewer and all of it travels with the file.
understanding.p2: This tool shows all of it, says which parts identify you, and removes them by rewriting the file around the image rather than re-saving the image: the compressed picture is copied byte for byte, so nothing is lost. Everything happens in your browser — the photo is never uploaded.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is my photo uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The file is read and rewritten inside your browser, and the page makes no request while it does. The one exception is the map link, which sends the coordinates to OpenStreetMap only if you click it.
faq.q2: Does removing the metadata lower the quality?
faq.a2: No. Most tools strip metadata by decoding the picture and saving it again, which recompresses a JPEG and loses detail every time. This one takes the file apart at its blocks, drops the metadata blocks and copies the compressed image unchanged, so every pixel is identical.
faq.q3: Why keep the colour profile and the orientation?
faq.a3: Neither says anything about you. The profile tells a screen how to show the colours, and a wide-gamut photo without it looks washed out. The orientation is one number saying the photo was stored sideways; without it a phone photo opens rotated. Both can be turned off if you want the file completely bare.
faq.q4: Do social networks remove this already?
faq.a4: The big ones usually strip GPS from what other people download, but they read it first, and messaging apps, email, cloud links and file transfers send the original untouched. Removing it yourself is the only way to be sure.
faq.q5: Why can it read HEIC but not clean it?
faq.a5: In HEIC, AVIF and TIFF the metadata sits in boxes whose byte positions are written into the rest of the file, so removing one means recalculating every offset after it. Getting that wrong produces a file that will not open, so the tool refuses rather than risk it. Convert the photo to JPEG first, then clean that.
faq.q6: What exactly is removed?
faq.a6: EXIF (with GPS and any embedded thumbnail), XMP, IPTC, JPEG comments, PNG text and timestamp chunks, maker-specific blocks, a JFIF thumbnail, and anything stored after the end of the image — where some phones hide a second picture or a video. What stays is what is needed to show the picture.

History stays in your browser.

understanding.title: Why a fast line can still freeze your calls
understanding.p1: A speed test that reports one big number answers the question nobody really has. A 100 Mbps line streams 4K easily and can still freeze a video call the moment someone else starts a download, because what breaks a call is not bandwidth but how long each packet waits in a queue when the line is busy. That waiting is called bufferbloat, and ordinary speed tests never measure it.
understanding.example: Download 96 Mbps · Idle 14 ms → busy 312 ms · Lag under load: D · Video calls: struggles
understanding.p2: This test measures latency while the line is idle and again while it is downloading and uploading, grades the difference, and turns the numbers into plain verdicts: 4K, calls, gaming, uploads. It compares the result with the plan you pay for, and keeps every run in your browser so you can see whether your line slows down in the evening.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Where does the test traffic go?
faq.a1: To Cloudflare's speed test servers at speed.cloudflare.com, from whichever of their locations is nearest to you — there is one in Dhaka. A test against a nearby server measures your own line rather than the distance to somebody's data centre. Cloudflare sees your IP address, as any website does; the results themselves are not reported back to them or to us.
faq.q2: What is lag under load?
faq.a2: The extra delay your connection adds when it is busy. A router with large buffers queues packets instead of dropping them, so a call's audio waits behind a download. The grade measures how much latency grows under load: A+ under 5 ms, A under 30, B under 60, C under 200, D under 400, and F beyond that. A router with SQM or Smart Queue Management usually turns an F into an A.
faq.q3: Why is my result lower than my plan?
faq.a3: Wi-Fi is the commonest reason: walls, distance and a crowded channel cost more than most lines lose. Other tabs and devices using the connection, an old phone or laptop, a VPN, and the time of day all play a part. Test over a cable, with nothing else running, at a few different times before you call your ISP — and use the history to show them when it is slow.
faq.q4: How much data does a test use?
faq.a4: It depends on the line, because the test keeps sending larger files until each takes about a second. A slow connection uses a few megabytes; a fast one can move a few hundred. On a capped mobile plan, run it sparingly.
faq.q5: Is my history sent anywhere?
faq.a5: No. Each finished run — the time, the speeds and the latencies — is kept in this browser's local storage and nowhere else, as is your plan. Clearing the history removes it.
faq.q6: How accurate is it?
faq.a6: It uses the measurement engine behind speed.cloudflare.com: several file sizes in each direction, timings from the browser's own Resource Timing API so page overhead is excluded, the 90th percentile of the download and upload samples, and the median of twenty idle latency samples. It measures the path to Cloudflare's nearest server, which is close to, but not exactly, the path to every site you use.

meta.title: Visual Mock Server Studio — Build Mock APIs Without Writing JSON
meta.description: Build mock REST APIs by dragging nodes onto a canvas instead of hand-writing JSON. Workspaces need no account: a secret in your browser proves ownership and a recovery key moves it to another machine. Mock endpoints answer from our servers, so they keep working after you close the tab.

hero.title: Mock Server Studio
hero.subtitle: Design an API before it exists: build each endpoint as a graph and point your app at a real URL that answers.
hero.disclosureTitle: This part does not run in your browser
hero.disclosureBody: Every other tool on ToolForge works entirely on your machine. This one cannot: a mock endpoint has to answer requests from your app, so your workspaces, endpoints and their responses are stored on our servers and served from them. A private server answers only callers holding its access token, an open one answers anyone with the address — either way, treat what you put in a response as public, and never put a real credential in one.

flow.title: From nothing to a live endpoint
flow.intro: Seven steps, and only the first two are about the studio itself. Everything after that is you describing the API you wish existed.
flow.example: GET /users/42 → the status, headers and JSON body you wrote for that route, after the delay you set
flow.workspaceBody: A workspace is the container for everything else — your mock servers, their routes, their variables and their request log. There is no email and no password: a secret written into an HttpOnly cookie is what proves this browser owns it.
flow.recoveryKeyBody: It is shown once, on the screen straight after creation, and only a one-way digest of it is stored — so nobody, us included, can show it to you again. It is how you reach the same workspace from another machine, and the only way back after you clear this browser's cookies.
flow.serverBody: A server owns a group of routes and answers on its own address. The key is the part callers type; leave it blank and one is drawn from the name. The address starts answering the moment the server has a route.
flow.routeBody: Pick a method and a path. A segment written as :name becomes a parameter, a trailing star matches everything below a prefix, and the query string is not part of the path — a route on /game answers /game?id=7 as well.
flow.responseBody: The response is built as a tree of fields rather than typed as JSON. Each field says where its value comes from: a fixed literal, something out of the request, a variable, or generated data such as a name, an email address, or a fresh UUID on every call.
flow.logicTitle: Put logic in front of it, if you need any
flow.logicBody: A route with no flow simply returns its body. Open the flow editor to add authentication, conditions, delays, weighted branches, variables and logging between the request arriving and the reply going out.
flow.callTitle: Point your app at the address
flow.callBody: Copy the address, call it from your code or from curl, and the calls appear in the workspace's request log. It answers whether or not this page is open, so a deployed front end can reach it too.
flow.outro: Make a server private and only callers holding its access token reach it — but a token can leak, and the data is stored on our servers, so treat everything in a response as public and never put a real credential in one.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need an account to use the Mock Server Studio?
faq.a1: No. Creating a workspace writes a secret into this browser and hands you a recovery key; between them, those are the whole of ownership. There is no email, no password and nothing to verify.
faq.q2: Does a mock endpoint keep answering after I close the tab?
faq.a2: Yes. Endpoints are served from our servers rather than from your browser, so a deployed front end or a colleague's machine can call them whether or not this page is open.
faq.q3: Can anybody else call my mock endpoints?
faq.a3: Not while the server is private: a call without its access token in the X-ToolForge-Key header gets a 401, and learns nothing about the server. Open it, and anybody holding the address can. Either way, treat everything in a response as public and never put a real credential, key or customer record in one.
faq.q4: What happens if I lose my recovery key?
faq.a4: Any browser that already owns the workspace keeps working, so the fastest fix is to open it on one of those. If none is left, the workspace cannot be recovered — only a one-way digest of the key is stored, so nobody can look it up or reissue it.
faq.q5: Can a response return different data on every call?
faq.a5: Yes, and that is most of the point. Fake data, UUIDs, the current time and One of fields all resolve per call, and a random branch can vary which response is reached at all.
faq.q6: How do I make a route fail, or be slow?
faq.a6: Add a Response node carrying the status you want and route to it — through a Condition to fail for particular input, or through a Random branch to fail a set share of calls. A Delay node in front of it models a slow service.
faq.q7: Can I take my work somewhere else?
faq.a7: Yes. Export this server gives a JSON bundle carrying every route, its response and its flow, and there is an OpenAPI export for describing the API to other tools. The bundle is the one that round-trips; the OpenAPI cannot carry generated values.

understanding.title: What a hex editor actually shows you
understanding.p1: Every file is a run of bytes. A text editor guesses which encoding those bytes are in and shows you characters; a hex editor does not guess. It shows you the bytes themselves, sixteen to a row, written as two hexadecimal digits each — and beside them, the same bytes read as ASCII so the parts that happen to be text are still readable.
understanding.p2: That is why a hex editor is what you reach for when a file will not open. A PNG that a viewer rejects starts with 89 50 4E 47 when it is intact; a JSON file that a parser refuses often begins with EF BB BF, a byte order mark nothing told you about. Neither is visible in an editor that is busy rendering characters.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is my file uploaded anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The file is read into your browser tab and every edit happens in memory. There is no server involved and no request that carries the contents anywhere, which is why the tool works with the network disconnected.
faq.q2: Can I insert or delete bytes rather than overwriting them?
faq.a2: Not in this editor. Every edit overwrites, so the file's length never changes — Delete writes zeroes rather than removing bytes, and Backspace zeroes the byte behind the caret. Insertion changes every offset after it, which for most of what a hex editor is used for is a way to break a file rather than to fix one.
faq.q3: Why does the scrollbar move in jumps on a very large file?
faq.a3: Browsers stop rendering an element past roughly 33.5 million pixels, which a file over about 24 MB would need. Past that size the scroll position is mapped onto the file by ratio, so one notch of the wheel covers more than one row. The keyboard and Go To still land on an exact byte, and the status bar always says which one the caret is on.
faq.q4: How large a file can it open?
faq.a4: Up to {max} MB. Larger files are refused by name rather than being half-read: the bytes are held whole so that reading one stays instant, and a tab holding much more than that is one the browser will kill.
faq.q5: Why does Save sometimes download a copy instead of saving the file?
faq.a5: Because the browser has no way to write back. Only browsers with the File System Access API can hand a page a writable handle to a file you picked, and a file dropped onto the page never comes with one. Where there is no handle, an edited copy through the download flow is the honest outcome, and the editor says so above the grid before you press anything.
faq.q6: What is the difference between the two byte orders in the inspector?
faq.a6: Which end of a multi-byte value comes first. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first, which is what x86 and ARM machines write; big-endian puts the most significant byte first, which is what most network protocols use. The bytes 01 02 03 04 are 67305985 one way and 16909060 the other — same bytes, different number.

meta.title: Hosted JSON Server — A Real REST API From One db.json
meta.description: Paste a db.json and get a hosted REST API with full CRUD, filtering, sorting, pagination and relations — the json-server you know, without leaving a laptop running. Private by default behind an access token. No account: a secret in your browser proves ownership and a recovery key brings the server back anywhere.

hero.title: JSON Server, hosted
hero.subtitle: Write or upload a db.json and get a json-server REST API that keeps answering after you close the laptop.
hero.disclosureTitle: This one does not run in your browser
hero.disclosureBody: Almost everything on ToolForge works entirely in your tab. This cannot: a page has no way to answer somebody else's HTTP request, so your document is stored on our servers and served from there. That means we hold your data, and anyone holding the server's access token — or anyone at all, if you open it — can read and change it. Treat a JSON server as a fixture for prototyping, never as somewhere to put anything real.

flow.title: From a db.json to a live API
flow.intro: Six steps, and only one of them differs from running json-server on your laptop — this one keeps answering after you close it.
flow.example: a db.json with a posts array → GET /posts/1, POST /posts, GET /posts?_page=2&_sort=title — all derived, none of it configured
flow.documentBody: The box on this page already holds json-server's own example document, so you can press Create and have something to call straight away. Replace it with your own whenever you like — every top-level key becomes a resource.
flow.createBody: Give it a name, and an address if you want to choose one; leave the address blank and one is generated. The address is the part that appears in the URL your client calls.
flow.recoveryKeyBody: It is shown once, right after the server is created, and only a hash of it is stored — so it cannot be shown again or looked up. It is how you reach this server from a browser that does not already own it, including this one after you clear cookies.
flow.routesBody: The Routes tab lists every path the document publishes, derived from the document rather than authored. If a route is on that list it answers; if a key publishes nothing, the tab names it and says why.
flow.callTitle: Point a client at the address
flow.callBody: Copy the base address and call it from fetch, curl, an HTTP client, or a front end you have deployed. Nothing has to be running on your machine.
flow.watchBody: The Requests tab shows the most recent calls the server answered. The Data tab is the live document — editing it there replaces everything at once, which is the same thing a client does one record at a time — and Download db.json takes it away.
flow.outro: A new server is private: a call without its access token in the X-ToolForge-Key header gets a 401. Open it and anybody with the address can read and change the document. Either way it is a fixture for prototyping, never somewhere to put anything real.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need an account?
faq.a1: No. Creating a server writes a secret into this browser and hands you a recovery key; between them, those are the whole of ownership. Nothing to verify and no password to choose.
faq.q2: How is this different from running json-server locally?
faq.a2: The behaviour is the same — same routes, same query language, same shapes. The difference is that this one keeps answering after you close the laptop, so a deployed front end, a phone on another network or a teammate can reach the same fixture.
faq.q3: Is my data private?
faq.a3: From strangers, yes, while the server is private: a call without its access token in the X-ToolForge-Key header gets a 401. But the document is stored on our servers, and a token pasted into a public front end can be read by whoever opens it — so use it for prototyping fixtures and never for anything real.
faq.q4: What happens when the document fills up?
faq.a4: POST, PUT and PATCH answer 507 while GET, DELETE and OPTIONS keep working, so deleting records you no longer need is the way back. The usage bar warns you well before that point.
faq.q5: Can I still use my db.json locally?
faq.a5: Yes. Download db.json gives you the current document as a file, and it is an ordinary db.json — run json-server against it and you get the same API on your own machine.
faq.q6: Why did my filter return nothing, or everything?
faq.a6: A local json-server drops a filter it cannot parse and returns the whole collection; here that answers 400 instead, so a typo is visible rather than silent. If a well-formed filter returns nothing, check the value's type: a numeric-looking value is compared as a number, so ?code=007 will not match the text 007.
faq.q7: What happens to related records when I delete one?
faq.a7: Foreign keys in other collections that pointed at the deleted record are set to null, whether or not you asked. Add _dependent with the collection name to remove those children instead of leaving them orphaned.

article.introBody: You give it a JSON document; it gives you a GraphQL endpoint. Every top-level key holding an array of objects becomes a type with a list field, a by-id field, a page envelope and four mutations. Every lone object becomes a type you can read and replace. Every foreign key becomes a relation you can follow from either end.
article.introSibling: Nothing is configured and nothing is generated into a file — the schema is derived from the document on every request, so it is never out of step with the data. The JSON Server Studio serves the same document as REST; the two run side by side on the same file, and a document sorted through one comes back in the same order through the other.

faq.q1: Who can call the endpoint?
faq.a1: A new server is private: only requests carrying its access token in the X-ToolForge-Key header are answered, and everything else gets a 401. Switch it to open from the access panel if you want anyone with the address to query it and run its mutations — handy for a quick demo, wrong for anything private. Pause the server when you are not using it; it then answers 503 rather than serving.
faq.q2: Can I use it with Apollo, urql or graphql-codegen?
faq.a2: Yes. Introspection is on, the SDL is a normal GraphQL schema using the standard scalars plus one JSON scalar, and the studio offers both schema.graphql and the introspection JSON as downloads. Point apollo client:download-schema or graphql-codegen at the endpoint and it works like any other server.
faq.q3: Why did my query come back as too costly?
faq.a3: The estimate multiplies each list field's page size down the query tree, so nesting three ten-item lists is a thousand nodes before any field is read. Narrow it with a smaller perPage, a where filter, or fewer nested relations. Every response carries x-graphql-cost, so you can see what a query costs before it becomes a problem.
faq.q4: Why is my Post type called Postt, or my people collection called Peopl?
faq.a4: The inflector guessed wrong. It carries the common irregulars but it is not a dictionary, and the studio prints the derived name beside every key so a wrong guess is visible. Rename the key in your document to something it reads correctly — the schema follows the document, always.
faq.q5: Can I add a field through a mutation?
faq.a5: No. The input types hold the fields the collection already has, so a value of the wrong shape is refused at validation rather than stored and discovered later. To add a field, edit the document in the Document tab and save — the schema rebuilds from it immediately.
faq.q6: Does it support subscriptions?
faq.a6: No. A subscription needs a transport that stays open and a source of events, and a stored fixture has neither. A schema that advertised subscriptions and never fired one would be worse than saying so.
faq.q7: What happens if I stop using it?
faq.a7: Nothing is deleted automatically today, but this is a free fixture service and dormant servers may be swept in future. Anything you would mind losing belongs somewhere else — and the document is one download away in the Document tab.
faq.q8: Can the same document be served as REST and GraphQL at once?
faq.a8: Not from one server, but the two studios read the same db.json, so you can paste one document into both and compare. They deliberately agree on the things that could otherwise differ: how records sort, how ids are generated and coerced, what counts as a collection, and where the size ceiling is.

understanding.title: What a keyboard tester tells you
understanding.p1: It lights each key you press and keeps it lit once it has worked, so a dead key is the one left dark. It also watches how keys arrive, which is where the faults people actually hit — doubled letters, blocked chords — show up.
understanding.example: E down 0 ms → E up 8 ms → E down 22 ms → one press, two letters: chatter, caught at 22 ms press to press
understanding.p2: Keys are matched by KeyboardEvent.code, the physical position, not the character it types. So the test means the same in a German, French or Bangla layout, and there is no need to switch to English first.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need to switch to the English layout?
faq.a1: No. Keys are matched by their physical position, so the test works the same in any layout. Where the browser can read your layout, the caps are even labelled from it.
faq.q2: Why does the Fn key never light up?
faq.a2: The keyboard handles Fn itself and never tells the computer. Press Fn with a media key instead: if the media key shows up under Other keys, Fn works.
faq.q3: Why can’t I test Ctrl+W or the Windows key?
faq.a3: The browser or the system acts on them before a page can. Use Capture system keys in Chrome or Edge, which hands them to the test while in full screen.
faq.q4: Is a red key definitely broken?
faq.a4: Red means at least one press arrived twice within the fault window. One is a hint; several are a switch that needs cleaning or replacing. Type the letter a few dozen times to be sure.
faq.q5: What does stopping at six keys mean?
faq.a5: The board reports six keys besides the modifiers at once — 6-key rollover, or USB boot mode on a board that can do more. Some boards switch to n-key rollover with a key combination; check its manual.
faq.q6: How do I leave the test with the keyboard?
faq.a6: Hold Escape for a second and a half, or click anywhere outside the board.
faq.q7: Is anything sent anywhere?
faq.a7: No. Every key is read and judged in this tab, and the report is written there too.

understanding.title: What a mouse tester tells you
understanding.p1: It counts what your mouse sends when you press, hold and scroll, and says whether that matches what your hand did. A healthy switch sends one press per press; a worn one sometimes sends two.
understanding.example: press 0 ms → release 6 ms → press 9 ms → one finger, two clicks: chatter, caught at 9 ms press to press
understanding.p2: The capture area is what makes the test possible. Inside it the side buttons cannot send the page back, the right button opens no menu and the wheel scrolls nothing, so you can press everything as often as you like and only the counters move.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why doesn’t the Back button take me back?
faq.a1: Inside the capture area it is cancelled, so you can press it as often as the test needs. Outside the area it works as usual.
faq.q2: Is a chatter reading proof the switch is broken?
faq.a2: One reading is a hint; several are a pattern. That is why one fault makes a button suspect and three make it faulty. Repeat the test on the flagged button before deciding.
faq.q3: Why does my polling rate read 60 or 144?
faq.a3: Your browser is not providing coalesced pointer events, so the tester can only sample once per frame — and the frame rate is what it measures. Try a current Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
faq.q4: Can this fix a double-clicking mouse?
faq.a4: No page can — the fault is in the switch. What it can do is tell you which switch and how often, which is what a warranty claim or a repair needs.
faq.q5: Why is my tilt wheel not part of the wheel verdict?
faq.a5: A tilt is a pair of switches, not an encoder, so it cannot jump back. Its presses are counted in the tiles; the wheel verdict covers up and down only.
faq.q6: Is anything sent anywhere?
faq.a6: No. Every event is read and judged in this tab, and the report is written there too.
faq.q7: Can I test a mouse on my phone?
faq.a7: Yes, if a mouse is connected to it by USB-OTG or Bluetooth. Taps on the screen are not counted.

understanding.title: What a screen test shows you
understanding.p1: It fills your whole screen with one colour at a time, so a pixel that is not doing what it should has nowhere to hide. A dot that stays dark on white, or lit on black, is a fault in the panel rather than in the picture.
understanding.example: #000000 full screen → one bright green dot that stays put → a green sub-pixel stuck on
understanding.p2: Clean the screen first and look from about arm's length, then step through every colour: each fault shows up best on one of them. Everything is painted in your browser, and nothing flashes — a screen changes only when you ask it to.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: What is the difference between a dead, a stuck and a hot pixel?
faq.a1: A dead pixel never lights: it shows as a black dot on white and on every other colour. A stuck pixel has one or two of its red, green and blue sub-pixels permanently on, so it shows as a coloured dot, clearest on black. A hot pixel has all three stuck on and shows as a white dot on black. Dust looks similar but sits on the surface: its edge is soft, and it moves against the picture when you move your head.
faq.q2: I found one. What should I do?
faq.a2: Photograph it close up on the screen that shows it best, and note where it sits. Check the seller's return window first — it is usually the easiest remedy — then the maker's pixel policy, since many accept a few faulty pixels before they will replace a panel. A stuck pixel sometimes clears by itself after the screen has been on for a while; a dead one does not. Do not press on the panel, which can make it worse.
faq.q3: Why is there no stuck-pixel fixer?
faq.a3: Fixers flash colours many times a second, and flashing more than three times a second can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy. The evidence that they revive stuck pixels is thin, so this test never flashes: a screen changes only when you press a key, click or tap.
faq.q4: The gradient shows steps. Is my screen faulty?
faq.a4: Faint, evenly spaced steps are normal: most screens show 256 shades from black to white, which is several pixels per shade across a wide display. Hard bands, uneven steps or a colour tint point at a 6-bit panel, a colour profile or a brightness setting such as dynamic contrast — turn those off and look again.
faq.q5: What is the checkerboard for?
faq.a5: It alternates black and white on every physical pixel, drawn at your screen's own resolution. From arm's length it should look like an even grey. Shimmer, crawling lines or a moiré pattern mean the picture is being scaled — the display is not at its native resolution — or the panel flickers under that pattern.
faq.q6: Why doesn't it go full screen on my iPhone?
faq.a6: Safari on the iPhone gives web pages no full-screen mode, so the test fills the window instead and says so. Turn the phone sideways, or add this site to your Home Screen and open it from there: it then runs without Safari's bars. iPads and other phones go full screen as usual.

understanding.title: What a refresh rate tester measures
understanding.p1: It times the frames your browser draws. A browser draws once per screen refresh, so the gap between frames is the refresh period, and the frames in a second are the refresh rate.
understanding.example: 6.94 ms between frames → 144.0 Hz — and one gap of 13.9 ms is one dropped frame, not a slower screen
understanding.p2: It reads the browser’s pace, which is the screen’s unless something holds it back: a battery saver, a low-power mode, or a browser that keeps pages at 60. Nothing is sent anywhere — every frame is timed in this tab.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why does it read 60 Hz on my 120 or 144 Hz screen?
faq.a1: Check the display’s own setting first — on Windows under Settings › System › Display › Advanced display, on a Mac under System Settings › Displays. If that says 144, something between the screen and the page is capping it: Safari has long kept web pages at 60 frames a second on ProMotion screens, and remote desktops and screen sharing often do the same.
faq.q2: Why does it read 30 Hz?
faq.a2: A battery saver is holding the browser back. Chrome’s Energy Saver and Low Power Mode on an iPhone or iPad both keep pages at about 30 frames a second. Plug in or switch the mode off and the reading comes back.
faq.q3: Which screen does it measure when I have two?
faq.a3: The one the browser window is on. Drag the window to the other screen and the reading follows within a few seconds, because it only covers the last five. If it never changes, your system or browser is pacing every window to one screen, which some setups with mixed refresh rates do.
faq.q4: Does it work with G-Sync, FreeSync or other adaptive sync?
faq.a4: It measures whatever the screen is doing. A browser normally draws at the screen’s maximum rate, so that is what it reads. Where adaptive sync is active for the browser window, a late frame makes the screen wait instead of skipping a refresh, so the reading dips and jitter rises rather than a dropped frame being counted.
faq.q5: What are dropped frames and jitter?
faq.a5: A dropped frame is a refresh the browser missed: a gap twice the usual length is one drop, three times is two. A few while the page loads or you switch windows are normal; a steady count means the computer or the browser cannot keep up. Jitter is how much the on-time gaps differ from each other — a fraction of a millisecond on a healthy system.
faq.q6: Why does it read 59.94 or 143.9 instead of a round number?
faq.a6: Many panels really run slightly off the number on the box — 59.94 Hz is an old television rate plenty of laptops still use — and browsers round their frame times, which the reading averages out over five seconds. The nearest common rate beside it is the name of the mode you are in.
faq.q7: What should I look for in the motion test?
faq.a7: Smoothness. At 960 px/s the block jumps 16 px between refreshes at 60 Hz and under 7 px at 144 Hz, so a faster screen looks visibly smoother. A stutter is a dropped frame. A blurred or doubled trail behind the block is the panel’s response time, or how your eyes follow motion — not the refresh rate.

understanding.title: What a webcam test shows
understanding.p1: It opens your camera in this tab and reads back what the camera is really sending: its size, its frame rate and its shape. If the picture appears, the camera, its cable, its driver and the browser's permission all work.
understanding.example: ask for 1920 × 1080 → the camera sends 1280 × 720 at 30 fps, 16:9 — its largest mode, not a fault
understanding.p2: What you ask for is a preference, not an order. The browser opens the camera in the mode nearest to it and the report shows that mode — which is how you find out whether a camera sold as 1080p really is.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is the video recorded or sent anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The picture goes from the camera to this tab and nowhere else. A snapshot is drawn in the tab and saved straight to your downloads.
faq.q2: Why does the camera list only say Default camera?
faq.a2: Browsers hide device names until a page is allowed to use the camera. Press Start camera and allow access, and the list fills in with every camera connected.
faq.q3: Why did I get 720p when I asked for 1080p?
faq.a3: The camera has no 1080p mode, or none the browser can use. Many laptop cameras stop at 720p. Choose Largest available to see the biggest mode it offers.
faq.q4: It says the camera is busy. What now?
faq.a4: Another app is holding it — a video call, a camera app or another browser tab. On Windows only one app can use a camera at a time. Close the others and press Start camera again.
faq.q5: I blocked the camera by mistake. How do I allow it again?
faq.a5: Click the icon at the left of the address bar, set the camera to Allow and reload the page. If it is allowed there and still blocked, the privacy settings on macOS or Windows are blocking the browser itself.
faq.q6: Why is the picture choppy when the frame rate says 30?
faq.a6: The figure is the rate the camera was set to, not a count of the frames that arrived. In a dim room many webcams lengthen each exposure and send fewer frames than the setting says. More light usually fixes it.
faq.q7: Why does the preview look mirrored?
faq.a7: It is flipped so that moving left moves you left, as in a mirror. People on a call see the unmirrored picture; turn off Mirror the preview to see that version.

verdict.quiet: Quiet — move closer to the microphone, or raise its input level in the system sound settings.
verdict.clipping: Clipping — the loudest sounds are being cut off. Move back a little, or lower the input level.

workbench.processingHint: Calls usually have all three on. Changing one reopens the microphone.

understanding.title: What a microphone test shows
understanding.p1: It opens your microphone in this tab and shows what reaches the browser: how loud it is, in dBFS, and how the sound spreads from low to high frequencies. If the meter moves when you speak, the microphone, its cable, its driver and the browser's permission all work.
understanding.example: speak at a normal distance → RMS around −20 dBFS, peaks near −8 dBFS — a good level; a peak at 0 dBFS is clipping
understanding.p2: Calls clean the sound up before sending it, with echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain. Turn them off to hear what the microphone itself picks up, and record a clip each way to compare.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is my voice recorded or sent anywhere?
faq.a1: No. The sound goes from the microphone to this tab and nowhere else. A clip you record is held in the tab's memory, played back there, and discarded when you leave the page.
faq.q2: Why does the microphone list only say Default microphone?
faq.a2: Browsers hide device names until a page is allowed to use the microphone. Press Start microphone and allow access, and the list fills in with every microphone connected.
faq.q3: What is dBFS, and what level should I aim for?
faq.a3: Decibels relative to full scale: 0 dBFS is the loudest a digital signal can be, so every reading below it is negative. Normal speech should read about −30 to −12 dBFS RMS, with peaks staying below about −3. A full-scale tone reads −3 dBFS RMS here, as in most audio software.
faq.q4: The meter does not move. What is wrong?
faq.a4: Something before the browser is silent: a mute switch on the headset or its cable, the input level turned all the way down in the system sound settings, or a different microphone chosen than the one you are speaking into. Pick the right one in the list, then check the system's input settings.
faq.q5: It says the microphone is busy. What now?
faq.a5: Another app is holding it — a call, a recorder or another browser tab — or its driver would not start. Close the others and press Start microphone again. Unplugging a USB headset and plugging it back in often helps too.
faq.q6: Why does my voice sound different with the processing off?
faq.a6: With it on, the browser removes echo and steady noise and evens out your level, which is what people on a call hear. With it off you hear the microphone itself: usually more background noise, and a level that rises and falls with your distance. Some browsers ignore a switch; the report shows what was really applied.
faq.q7: Why can't I hear myself live while I speak?
faq.a7: Playing the microphone straight back through the speakers would loop into the microphone and howl. Record a clip and play it back instead — through headphones you hear exactly what was captured.

meta.title: ToolForge MCP Server — Connect Claude and ChatGPT
meta.description: Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client to ToolForge. One HTTP endpoint exposes encoding, hashing, encryption, JWT, formatting, text and domain tools as callable tools.

hero.title: Use ToolForge from your assistant
hero.subtitle: Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client to one address and call ToolForge's tools by name.

connect.quotaMissing: This deployment cannot serve MCP yet. The endpoint meters every caller, and metering needs both a database and MCP_IP_SALT — without them it refuses every request rather than running unmetered. Set both, then reload this page.
connect.endpointBody: One endpoint, for every client and every tool. It speaks Streamable HTTP and it is stateless: no session to open, nothing to keep alive, and no id to lose when a serverless instance is recycled.
connect.endpointTransport: Set the transport to HTTP, not SSE — the older Server-Sent Events transport is a different shape and this endpoint does not answer it.
connect.clientsBody: Every offline tool works with nothing but the address. A token is only needed for the tools that make outbound requests, and those are named further down.
connect.probeBody: One request, no client. A working endpoint answers with its name, version and protocol version.
connect.tokenBody: Most of what ToolForge exposes is arithmetic on your own input — encoding, hashing, parsing — and costs this deployment a few milliseconds of CPU. Those tools are open to anyone, bounded by the rate limit rather than by a password.
connect.tokenScope: One tool is different. The domain inspector reaches other people's hosts, from this server's address, with this site's name on the packets. Left open, that is a scanner a stranger's assistant can drive. So it is gated on a bearer token — and when no token is configured it is refused rather than served, because a gate that opens when its configuration is missing is not a gate.
connect.tokenPresent: This deployment has a token configured. Networked tools will work for a client that sends it.
connect.tokenAbsent: This deployment has no MCP_ACCESS_TOKEN set. Every offline tool works; the domain inspector will refuse with token_missing until one is configured.
connect.tokenRotate: Rotating it is a one-line change and takes effect on the next request — the value is read from the environment per call, not captured at startup. Clients holding the old token start failing immediately, which is the point.
connect.tokenPath: The token is only ever sent as an Authorization header to {path}. It never appears in a URL, so it cannot end up in browser history, a proxy log or a Referer header.

tools.body: {count} tools, all running on the server. Every one of them is the same code the tool page runs, so an answer here and an answer there cannot disagree.

what.title: What this is
what.p1: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way for an assistant to call something that is not itself. A client connects to a server, asks what tools it has, and from then on the model can call them — with arguments it chose, and results it reads before answering you.
what.example: You: decode this JWT and tell me when it expires → the assistant calls toolforge_jwt_decode → it answers from the real claims, not from a guess
what.p2: That last part is the difference worth understanding. A model asked to base64-decode a string will often produce something that looks right and is wrong in the middle. A model that calls a decoder gets the actual bytes. The same holds for a hash, a cron expression, a diff, or the expiry on a certificate.
what.p3: Everything here runs on the ToolForge server rather than in your browser, which is a real departure from how the rest of this site works — the tool pages do their work in the tab and upload nothing. Over MCP, whatever you pass as an argument reaches this server, and the tools that reach the network reach it from here.

examples.title: What asking looks like
examples.p1: You do not name the tool. You ask for the thing, and the assistant picks — which is why every tool here carries a description written for a model choosing between thirty of them.

decode.runs: Calls toolforge_jwt_decode, reads exp against the clock, and warns you if the token is unsigned.

hash.ask: Hash this password with Argon2id at the OWASP settings
hash.runs: Calls toolforge_hash_generate with a freshly generated salt, and returns the encoded hash with its parameters inside it.

cron.runs: Calls toolforge_cron_explain, which returns real instants in that zone — and flags any run a daylight-saving jump would erase.

diff.ask: What changed between these two config files?
diff.runs: Calls toolforge_diff_compare and gets a unified patch back, which is far cheaper to read than two files side by side.

domain.runs: Calls toolforge_domain_inspector_inspect — the one tool that needs the token, because it reaches the host to find out.

limits.title: Limits
limits.p1: <address></address> calls a minute per caller, and <tool></tool> a minute per tool across everyone. The first bounds one client in a loop; the second bounds a flood spread across many, which no per-caller limit can do.
limits.p2: A refusal clears inside a minute and says when, in a Retry-After header and in the rate-limit headers on every answer. A client watching those sees its budget counting down before anything breaks.
limits.p3: Individual tools keep their own ceilings — the diff refuses documents past its line count, the QR encoder past what the specification can carry — and those are the same ceilings the tool pages hold.

absent.title: What is not here, and why
absent.p1: Six groups are missing on purpose. Each one is a fact about the tool rather than a gap in the endpoint, and toolforge_catalog_list returns the web address of every one of them so an assistant can send you to the page instead of reporting a dead end.

images.title: The image tools
images.body: The compressor, converter, resizer, blur placeholder and background remover decode pixels in a canvas and re-encode them through WebAssembly codecs built for a browser. There is no canvas in a request handler, and a server-side reimplementation would be a second encoder to keep in step with the first. The favicon generator is absent for the same reason: it draws its text on a canvas, in the reader's fonts and the reader's system emoji. The background remover adds a second reason: its segmentation weights are fetched into the reader's own browser and cached there, so running it here would move a hundred-megabyte download and the inference behind it onto this deployment for every call. Image to Text is absent for that second reason: its engine and language data are fetched into the reader's browser and run in a web worker there, so running it here would put seconds of recognition per picture onto this deployment for every call — and a model that wants the text in a picture can already read it.

studios.title: The server studios and the shortener
studios.body: Each of them mints a public address and stores what is posted to it, against an ownership model built on browser cookies. An MCP client has no cookie jar and no way to prove it owns what it created, so creating one here would mint something nobody could ever reclaim.

ai.title: The AI tools
ai.body: The watermark remover's picture tab spends a third-party API budget on every call. That is a decision about money rather than about capability, and it belongs to whoever is paying. The watermark remover's video tab is absent for the images' reason instead: it demuxes, decodes, repaints and re-encodes a clip through the browser's own codecs, none of which exists in a request handler. Text to Speech is absent for a neighbouring reason: every generation is a request to Microsoft's speech service from this site's one address, and the page shares that service's patience between readers with a bot check and an hourly ceiling that a single token-holding caller would exhaust.

scanner.title: The port scanner
scanner.body: Its whole function is to touch somebody else's host on ports they did not offer. Behind a model that can be talked into things, a token is not the protection it looks like.

hardware.title: The hardware testers
hardware.body: The mouse and keyboard testers measure a physical device in a browser: the gaps between presses, the wheel, the keys held at once. An MCP call has no mouse or keyboard on the other end of it, and a tool that took a list of timestamps instead would be one nobody had a reason to call. The refresh rate tester times the frames a screen paces in a tab, and an MCP call has no screen behind it either. The same goes for the dead pixel and screen tester, whose only output is colour on the screen you are looking at. The webcam tester opens the camera on your own device, and an MCP call has no camera to open — nor the microphone tester a microphone to listen to.

connection.title: What Is My IP
connection.body: It reports the address a request arrived from. Over MCP that request comes from the assistant's host, not from you, so the answer would be somebody else's address presented as yours. Ask from a terminal with curl instead.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need an API key?
faq.a1: Not for most of it. Every offline tool — encoding, hashing, encryption, JWTs, formatting, diffing, colours, cron, timestamps — works with nothing but the address. Only the domain inspector asks for a bearer token, because it is the only one that makes outbound requests. Set MCP_ACCESS_TOKEN on the deployment and send it as Authorization: Bearer.
faq.q2: Is my data private here?
faq.a2: Less private than on the tool pages, and that is worth being exact about. A tool page does its work in your browser and uploads nothing. Over MCP, arguments travel to this server, are used, and are discarded — nothing is stored — but they also travel through your assistant, and whoever runs that assistant keeps the conversation. Do not pass a production secret through a chat you would not want retained.
faq.q3: Which MCP clients work?
faq.a3: Anything that speaks Streamable HTTP: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, claude.ai custom connectors, ChatGPT connectors in developer mode, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and the MCP Inspector. The older SSE transport is a different shape and is not served.
faq.q4: Why does my client show no tools?
faq.a4: Three usual causes. The transport is set to SSE rather than HTTP. The address is missing /api/mcp at the end. Or the deployment has no database and no MCP_IP_SALT, in which case the endpoint refuses every request — the banner at the top of this page says so when that is the case.
faq.q5: Can I run this against my own deployment?
faq.a5: Yes, and that is the intended arrangement for anything sensitive. ToolForge is MIT-licensed and self-hostable; point the client at your own host and both the token and the rate limit are yours to set.
faq.q6: Does calling a tool cost me anything?
faq.a6: No. There is no billing, no account and no sign-up. The rate limit exists so one caller cannot spend the whole deployment's budget, not to sell you a larger one.
